title: These Are The U.S. Weapons Most At Risk In The Looming Rare Earths Supply Crisis
zh_title: 这些是迫在眉睫的稀土供应危机中面临最大风险的美国武器
summary: 谷歌前首席执行官埃里克·施密特创立的智囊团的一份新报告量化了美国国防工业基地在关键稀土矿物方面依赖中国的严峻现实。它还详细说明了如果这种微妙的供应关系破裂，哪些武器系统可能面临最大的影响。这份白皮书专门从特别竞争研究项目中获得，利用供应链技术公司 Exiger 的人工智能情报来评估有多少种由国家物品识别码 (NIIN) 识别的独特组件含有关键矿物质，例如锑、g
content:
谷歌前首席执行官埃里克·施密特创立的智囊团的一份新报告量化了美国国防工业基地在关键稀土矿物方面依赖中国的严峻现实。它还详细说明了如果这种微妙的供应关系破裂，哪些武器系统可能面临最大的影响。这份白皮书专门从特别竞争研究项目中获得，利用供应链科技公司 Exiger 的人工智能情报来评估有多少由国家物品识别号 (NIIN) 识别的独特组件含有关键矿物质，例如锑、镓、锗和钨。美国的武器库依赖于稀土的稳定供应，尤其是最先进的武器。美国空军 摄影：Tech Sgt.托马斯·巴利科技。中士。 Thomas Barley 通过对近 900 万个零件和 3,000 个美国军用武器系统的评估，该公司在 1,400 个武器系统中发现了 28,000 多个独特组件仅含有这四种稀土。由于近期的危机，这些部分的隔离尤其重要：中国出口管制的暂停将于 11 月到期。根据白皮书，武器部署计划以及战备和保障活动很有可能受到干扰。然而，Exiger 首席战略和全球事务官基特·康克林 (Kit Conklin) 表示，危机已经到来。
在接受 TWZ 采访时，他指出日本正面临着生产停顿的前景，因为今年早些时候中国切断了一些稀土供应超过 80%。康克林表示：“毫无疑问，目前对于许多试图获得中国批准的许可证但没有获得许可证的公司来说，这是一场危机。” “因此，当前的生产存在真正的风险，当我考虑我们的生产和规模扩张时，无论是无人机工业基地还是试图将我们的拦截器产能扩大到每年 1,000、2,000、3,000 个拦截器，我的意思是，这些都是我们面临的真正的瓶颈，正在影响我们现在向作战人员提供这些拦截器的能力。”数据显示，供应链和制造中断风险最大的武器系统之一是至关重要的弗吉尼亚级潜艇，它需要 300 多个含有四种元素的关键 NIIN，其中包括 190 个需要锗的部件。弗吉尼亚号（SSN 774）是弗吉尼亚级的领舰，是美国海军快速攻击潜艇部队的骨干力量。美国海军照片由通用动力电船公司拍摄 美国海军锗是锌矿石的副产品，用于光学、夜视系统、EO/IR 设备等。一月份，五角大楼宣布投资 1800 万美元建设位于圣路易斯的美国唯一的锗生产设施。
犹他州乔治市将在未具体说明的期限内将炼油能力扩大“七倍”，达到每年 20 吨以上。中国控制着全球约 68% 的精炼锗。它对用于半导体和太阳能电池，尤其是先进雷达的镓的控制力要大得多，控制着高达 99% 的产量。每个弗吉尼亚级潜艇都需要 50 个含有镓的独特部件。中国控制着大约一半的锑产量，用于硬化弹药以及制造光学和电子产品；高达80%的钨供应量，用于制造工具、弹头和耐热部件。虽然它

【原文 English Original】
A new report from the think tank founded by former Google CEO Eric Schmidt quantifies the grim realities of the U.S. defense industrial base’s dependence on China for critical rare earth minerals. It also details which weapons systems might face the most impact if that delicate supply relationship breaks down. The white paper, exclusively obtained from the Special Competitive Studies Project, uses AI intelligence from the supply chain tech firm Exiger to assess how many unique components, identified by National Item Identification Number, or NIIN, contain critical minerals, such as antimony, gallium, germanium and tungsten. America’s arsenal depends on a steady flow of rare earths, and especially its most advanced weapons. U.S. Air Force photo by Tech Sgt. Thomas Barley Tech. Sgt. Thomas Barley From an assessment of almost nine million parts and 3,000 U.S. military weapon systems, the company identified more than 28,000 unique components  across 1,400 weapons systems containing just these four rare earths. The isolation of these parts is relevant in particular because of a near-term crisis: the expiration of a suspension on Chinese export controls set to take effect in November. Disruption to weapons fielding plans, as well as operational readiness and sustainment activities, according to the white paper, is very much a possibility. Yet according to Kit Conklin, chief strategy and global affairs officer at Exiger, the crisis is already here.  In an interview with TWZ , he pointed to Japan, which is facing the prospect of a manufacturing halt after China choked off supply of some rare earths to the tune of more than 80% earlier this year. “There’s no question that right now it’s a crisis for a lot of companies that are trying to get licenses approved by China and just not getting the licenses,” Conklin said. “So there’s real risk to current production, and when I think about us and scaling, whether it’s the drone industrial base or trying to scale our interceptor capacity to 1,000, 2,000, 3,000 interceptors a year, I mean, these are real choke points that we have that are impacting our ability to deliver these to the warfighter right now.” Among the weapons systems most at risk for supply chain and manufacturing disruption, according to the data, is the vital Virginia -class submarine, which requires more than 300 critical NIINs containing the four elements, including 190 parts requiring germanium. USS Virginia (SSN 774), the leader of the Virginia class that serves as the backbone of the U.S. Navy’s fast attack submarine force. U.S. Navy photo by General Dynamics Electric Boat U.S. Navy Germanium, used in optics, night vision systems, EO/IR equipment and more, is a byproduct of zinc ore . In January, the Pentagon announced an $18 million investment in the country’s only germanium production facility in St. George, Utah to expand refining capacity “sevenfold” to more than 20 metric tons annually by an unspecified deadline. China controls some 68% of the world’s refined germanium. It has a far greater chokehold on gallium, used in semiconductors and solar cells, and especially advanced radars, controlling up to 99% of production . Each Virginia -class sub requires 50 unique parts containing gallium. China controls about half the production of antimony, used to harden ammunition and to manufacture optics and electronics; and up to 80% of the supply of tungsten, used in manufacturing tools, warheads and heat-resistant components. While it doesn’t break down components by weight, the report notes that the rare earth requirements for the Virginia -class sub are also considerable by mass: each sub required 9,200 pounds of the elements, while an F-35 Joint Strike Fighter jet requires 900 pounds. Special Competitive Studies Project The Virginia -class submarine is America’s only in-production fast-attack nuclear-powered sub that has been in service since 2004. Twenty three of these critical vessels are in service today , or roughly half of the total planned program, with the remaining boats yet to be built. It’s notable in the context of the paper because it has multiple points of exposure to supply chain disruption. Another of these exposure points: its 1,700 mission or safety-critical parts requiring casting, forging or extrusion. As the report lays out, supply chain bottlenecks around limited metal casting, forging and extruding capacity are delaying production timelines and putting manufacturing at risk. China, again, produces about half of the world’s casting output and “is often the sole option for large castings,” the paper found. The analysis shows that more than half, or nearly 8,000, unique supply items containing steel castings have delivery lead times of more than 36 weeks. More than 9,400 items containing extruded aluminum, about 47% of these parts, have lead times that long. A large metal casting for a port crane. Voestalpine Foundry Group “ Virginia -class submarines, already threatened by U.S. reliance on China for critical minerals, are reportedly also three years behind schedule, potentially due in part to the lack of domestic large-scale casting capacity,” the report finds. An analysis of Navy construction timelines published earlier this year does indeed find that 10 of the 12 Virginia subs now under construction face delays of 36-44 months. Alarmingly, a recent war game simulation found that the U.S. could not replace ships, planes and missiles lost to combat specifically due to casting and forging shortfalls, the report notes. That’s despite a $2 billion Pentagon initiative launched in 2024 aimed at revitalizing this industry. Beyond submarines, the report shows that aircraft, including some of the nation’s workhorse fighter jets, face outsized production and sustainment risk due to rare-earth elements and casting/forging dependencies. The B-2 Spirit bomber – the nation’s only nuclear-armed stealth bomber until fielding begins on the B-21 Raider sometime next year – requires 782 parts containing the four rare-earth elements isolated in the report. Special Competitive Studies Project The F/A-18 Hornet family of fighters flown by the Navy and Marine Corps, including the Navy’s Growler electronic warfare variant, tops the list for dependency on steel castings, with 3,800 individual parts requiring the process. Following is the KC-135 Stratotanker, with 2,570 parts. All 10 of the systems requiring the most metal castings for production are aircraft, the analysis shows. The legacy Hornet and the KC-135 have been out of production for decades, while the Navy’s Super Hornet will see its production line go cold in 2027. Any ongoing demand for castings for these systems would thus be in spares and repair parts. Special Competitive Studies Project Military aircraft also represent the highest-need category among weapons systems requiring cadmium plating, a process used to make aerospace components corrosion-resistant.  The domestic supplier base has shrunk due to EPA safety limitations established in 2008. All of the top 10 weapons systems requiring the most cadmium-plated parts are aircraft, with the KC-135 topping the list with 2,780 unique components. The C-130 Hercules transport, B-52 Stratofortress bomber and Galaxy C-5 transport all have more than 2,000 parts. Special Competitive Studies Project The B-52, which is undergoing a service life extension to take it into the 2050s – past its century mark – may run into modernization delays not only over cadmium-plated and steel-casted components, but also due to overly rigid military specifications, which increase lead time and delays. The white paper cites the bomber’s rib airfoil and fuel vent valve components, which both have lead times of more than 400 days due in part to production being burdened with dozens of mil-spec compliance requirements, which the authors say have not kept pace with today’s commercial practices. “The requirement for a part to meet so many mil-specs, if not reasonably necessary, may limit the number of possible suppliers of that part, potentially increasing its lead time and bottlenecking production,” they write. “For the B-52, this could inhibit current modernization efforts intended to keep the airplane operational through the 2050s.” A B-52H Stratofortress undergoing programmed depot maintenance is towed into a hangar at Tinker Air Force Base, Oklahoma, July 28, 2025. U.S. Air Force photo by Paul Shirk Paul Shirk A final risk the paper addresses is workforce shortages and dangers from limited suppliers creating single points of failure. Across defense, the number of small suppliers has decreased by 43% in the last decade, it notes. It cites, as a case study, the February 2025 fire that forced the closure of SPS Technologies in Jenkintown, Penn. – a fastener maker that produced components for more than 1,000 weapons systems and was deemed critical for 90, including the Nimitz -class carrier, the F/A-18 fighter and the M1 Abrams tank. For systems including the Tomahawk Land Attack Missile and the MH-60 Black Hawk helicopter, the facility was a single-source supplier. With operations offline until at least 2028, the supply chain has been “actively disrupted” due to the outage of just one facility, according to the paper. “This case underscores the risk of single sourcing in the defense industrial base and the need to qualify alternate sources to avoid such significant chokepoints,” the authors write. The paper hails work that has already begun to invest in domestic critical minerals production and shore up the defense industrial base. But it does hint that these efforts may be too late to avoid a crash if China shuts off or severely reduces exports. The paper notes that, on average, it takes the U.S. 29 years to open a new mine. The U.S. has one established domestic mine: The Mountain Pass Rare Earth Mine and Processing Facility, just outside of Las Vegas. Initially established in 1952 and reopened in 2018 after a long hiatus, it now produces more than 50,000 tons of rare earth oxides annually . Last year, for the first time in seven decades, a new domestic rare-earth mine opened in Wyoming , stating plans to start producing ores extracted from coal, including gallium and germanium, by 2029 . Production is projected to total 456 tons of rare earths per year. The project had been in development for more than a decade before opening.  The Mountain Pass Rare Earth Mine and Processing Facility. MP Materials Conklin said a July executive order aimed at developing domestic production of rare earths while collecting data on what elements systems required created opportunities for smart policy creation – perhaps in the next National Defense Authorization Act – around holistically attacking the problem.  “I would love for us to figure out a way to get out of thinking about these supply chain risks system by system. We tend to have disparate requirements to look at the nuclear triad or subs or interceptors,” he said. “I think with the executive order that came out earlier this year, there’s a real opportunity for Congress to legislate on some of these issues beyond just figuring out what the risk [is] for antimony in the sub industrial base, and thinking about it a little bit more holistically.” One potential solution he proposed: an agency within the executive branch (led, perhaps, by a critical minerals czar) who can coordinate production needs and resourcing and develop the most efficient pathways to secure needed materials. There are few weapons that are not impacted by the scarcity of robust sources for rare earths. RTX While no U.S. defense manufacturer has yet publicly cited manufacturing disruptions due to rare earth availability, signs are increasing that the federal government is taking supply concerns seriously. In addition to Project Vault , a $12 billion White House initiative announced in February that would create a strategic stockpile of rare earths akin to existing stockpiles of critical medical supplies and petroleum, the U.S. Army has begun extending long-term leases on military land to companies seeking to build critical mineral processing facilities. Conklin said he doesn’t anticipate major changes in rare earth exports between now and the end of the year, describing the U.S.-China supply relationship as “in a bit of a détente.” That said, with new policies pending, we could be only days away from new revelations about the extent of the impact of these materials on the defense manufacturing enterprise. Contact the editor: Tyler@twz.com The post These Are The U.S. Weapons Most At Risk In The Looming Rare Earths Supply Crisis appeared first on TWZ .

title: How to prevent an energy quarantine of Taiwan
zh_title: 如何防止台湾能源检疫
summary: 如何防止台湾能源检疫 - 大西洋理事会北京正在为台湾能源检疫奠定基础。经济、政治、技术和军事因素可能导致能源检疫风险在 2028 年和 2029 年达到顶峰。为了阻止这种强制行动，美国及其盟国应与台湾合作，通过支持上述所有能源战略来加强其安全，重点是向台湾北部供应用于发电的柴油。中共总书记习近平多次明确表态：
content:
如何防止台湾能源检疫 - 大西洋理事会
北京正在为台湾的能源检疫奠定基础。
经济、政治、技术和军事因素可能导致能源检疫风险在 2028 年和 2029 年达到峰值。
为了阻止这种胁迫行动，美国及其盟国应与台湾合作，通过支持上述所有能源战略来加强台湾的安全，重点是向台湾北部供应用于发电的柴油。
中国共产党总书记习近平一贯明确表示台湾应该与中国大陆“统一”，并在2013年表示“两岸长期存在的政治分歧……总不能一代一代传下去”。习近平还在 2026 年 5 月与美国总统唐纳德·特朗普会面时警告称，在台湾问题上可能会发生“冲突甚至冲突”。这件事似乎不是决心的问题，而是时机的问题。出于政治、经济和技术原因，习近平可能对台湾采取行动的风险可能在 2028 年和 2029 年达到顶峰。
为了实现其长期的统一目标，北京可能会尝试通过非动能措施胁迫台湾。隔离的模糊性和灵活性可能使其成为对习近平特别有吸引力的选择。北京可以宣称，检疫——允许一些船只通过，同时拒绝其他船只，特别是油轮和液化天然气（LNG）运输船——是一种国内执法措施，而不是一种战争行为。有证据表明，习近平的军队已经在为隔离而不是入侵进行演练，因为中国海警在台湾以东海域持续存在，并试图将封锁商业交通正常化，从而挑战台北的海上控制。
切断台湾能源供应的隔离作为一种强制工具尤其有效。台湾几乎没有本土生产石油、天然气或煤炭，这使得它几乎完全依赖海运进口碳氢化合物。北京很早就明白能源安全在台湾突发事件中的重要性。目前，它不太容易受到能源中断的影响，并准备好承受根据需要切断部分能源进口的情况。
对台湾实施能源隔离对美国来说将是一件严重的事情。台湾因其地理位置、深厚的技术专长以及作为人工智能（AI）供应链关键节点的地位而对华盛顿具有重要的战略意义。中国吞并台湾将使全球经济和战略力量平衡向有利于北京的方向倾斜，美国决策者必须避免对台湾采取强制行动，否则可能升级为军事冲突。碰撞的危险怎么强调都不为过：美国和中国都是拥有强大常规军队的核武器国家；技术超级大国，尤其是人工智能领域；以及拥有一系列强制工具的庞大经济体。
应对这些风险需要大量军事投资，但联盟决策者不应忽视近期能源隔离的严重风险。为了阻止台湾的能源隔离，美国和其他民主国家应与台湾合作，通过上述所有方法以及快速部署燃料来源（特别是柴油）的战略优先事项来加强其能源安全。美国，T

【原文 English Original】
How to prevent an energy quarantine of Taiwan - Atlantic Council
Beijing is laying the groundwork for an energy quarantine of Taiwan.
Economic, political, technical, and military factors could lead energy quarantine risks to peak in 2028 and 2029.
To deter this coercive action, the United States and allies should work with Taiwan to bolster its security through support for an all-of-the-above energy strategy, concentrating on supplying northern Taiwan with diesel for power generation.
Chinese Communist Party (CCP) General Secretary Xi Jinping has consistently made clear his view that Taiwan should be “reunified” with mainland China, stating in 2013 that “long-standing cross-Strait political differences … cannot be passed down from generation to generation (总不能一代一代传下去).” Xi also warned of “clashes or even conflicts” over Taiwan in his May 2026 meeting with US President Donald Trump. The matter appears to be a question not of determination but of timing. For political, economic, and technical reasons, the risk that Xi might move against Taiwan could peak in 2028 and 2029.
To achieve its longstanding unification goal, Beijing might attempt to coerce Taiwan via non-kinetic measures. The ambiguity and flexibility of a quarantine could render it an especially attractive option for Xi. Beijing could claim that a quarantine—allowing some ships to pass while turning back others, especially oil tankers and liquefied natural gas (LNG) carriers—is a domestic law-enforcement measure rather than an act of war. There is some evidence that Xi’s forces are already rehearsing for a quarantine rather than an invasion, as the Chinese coast guard is maintaining a continuous presence in waters east of Taiwan and trying to normalize interdictions of live commercial traffic, thereby challenging Taipei’s maritime control.
A quarantine to cut off Taiwan’s energy supply would be particularly effective as a coercive tool. Taiwan has virtually no indigenous production of oil, natural gas, or coal, rendering it almost totally reliant on seaborne imports for hydrocarbons. Beijing has long understood the importance of energy security in a Taiwan contingency. It is currently much less vulnerable to an energy outage and is prepared to weather a cutoff of some of its own energy imports as needed.
An energy quarantine of Taiwan would be a grave matter for the United States. Taiwan is strategically important to Washington due to its geography, deep technological expertise, and position as a critical node in artificial intelligence (AI) supply chains. China’s absorption of Taiwan would tilt the global economic and strategic balance of power in Beijing’s favor, making it imperative for US policymakers to avert coercive action against the island, which could escalate into a military conflict. It is difficult to overstate the dangers of a collision: the United States and China are nuclear-armed nations with powerful conventional militaries; technological superpowers, especially in AI; and huge economies with an array of coercive tools.
Countering these risks will require substantial military investments, but coalition policymakers should not overlook the serious risks of a near-term energy quarantine. To deter an energy quarantine of Taiwan, the United States and other democracies should work with Taiwan to reinforce its energy security with an all-of-the-above approach and the strategic prioritization of rapidly deployable fuel sources, especially diesel. The United States, Taiwan, and other actors should immediately begin preparing for a contingency by deploying a diesel-generation supply chain across Taiwan, especially in the energy-scarce northern regions surrounding the capital, Taipei. That will include diesel production at refineries, distributed storage, and ultimately generators for power supply. The humble diesel generator could be a key determinant in the future of global power.
The groundwork: Beijing is mitigating its own energy vulnerabilities
In 2003, then General Secretary Hu Jintao warned that China faced the “Malacca Dilemma,” or “马六甲困局.” Hu noted that Beijing’s reliance on seaborne oil imports from the Middle East navigating the Malacca Strait near Singapore raised acute vulnerabilities, as shipments could be interdicted by the US Navy. More than two decades later, Beijing is becoming increasingly self-sufficient in energy overall and in transportation fuels such as gasoline, diesel, and jet fuel. While Beijing will not achieve true independence in transportation fuels for several years, it is on its way to effectively mitigating the Malacca Dilemma.
Beijing has been seeking to mitigate this dilemma via a combination of reduced transport fuel demand (largely from vehicle electrification), elevated domestic crude oil production, overland crude oil pipeline imports (largely from Russia), maximizing refinery production of transportation fuels, and tapping unprecedentedly large petroleum stockpiles. Beijing’s growing oil security will enable it to increasingly decouple from international markets and allow it to act more aggressively vis-à-vis Taiwan.
Electrification has been fundamental to China’s energy self-sufficiency drive. Electricity’s share of final energy in China has grown from about 5 percent in 1990 to nearly 30 percent today, an increase of about 1 percentage point every year, and will soon surpass the percentage share of every Group of Seven (G7) economy. Mainland China’s power generation capacity has risen from 138 gigawatts in 1990 to over 4,000 gigawatts by May 2026; China has also added 24.2 million charging points (not stations) and, by 2023, had already provided $230 billion in government support to its EV industry. Finally, many Chinese cities have mandated that ride share vehicles and urban logistics vehicles must be “new energy vehicles”—in practice, usually battery EVs. These measures have enabled China to become the undeniable world leader in vehicle electrification.
Vehicle electrification rapidly mitigates Beijing’s exposure to the Malacca Dilemma by directly reducing gasoline and diesel demand, especially in politically-sensitive first tier cities. According to the International Energy Agency, electric vehicles are set to reduce Chinese oil demand by about a total of 2.7 million barrels per day (MMbpd) by 2030. In a July 2025 analysis, Rhodium Group found that China’s total electric vehicle fleet already displaced more than 1 MMbpd, with battery electric vehicles beginning to make significant headway in trucking fleets that rely primarily on diesel.
For these reasons, the International Energy Agency and others hold that Chinese gasoline and diesel demand has likely already peaked. Deployment of advanced, energy-dense batteries to medium and heavy-duty vehicles would further reduce diesel consumption, alleviating Beijing’s chief transport fuel constraint in a crisis. Adoption of advanced batteries in heavy-duty vehicles might rise sharply over the next year or two.
As it reduces its transport fuel demand via vehicle electrification, China has also stockpiled about 1.2 billion barrels of crude oil in December 2025 in total petroleum reserves, by far the world’s largest. While Beijing is drawing down oil inventories amid the oil market disruptions from the US–Iran war, storage levels remain elevated and can be expanded if the conflict winds down.
In the case of a quarantine, Beijing would rely heavily on supply flows of oil, not only on stock withdrawals.
Here it’s useful to divide Beijing’s oil supplies into different resilience tiers. Tier 1, the most secure tier, is China’s own domestic crude oil production, which ticked up from 3.8 million barrels per day (MMbpd) in 2017 to about 4.4 MMbpd in the first seven months of 2026, covering about 30 percent of domestic demand before the US–Iran war.
In addition to its own domestic production, China can also obtain additional volumes from relatively secure overland pipelines in Tier 2A. China’s secure overland crude oil shipments total about 0.8 MMbpd. This is split between the Russia-to-China leg of the East Siberia–Pacific Ocean pipeline, with deliveries of about 600,000 barrels per day (b/d), and the Atasu–Alashankou pipeline, which brings both Russian and Kazakhstani oil via Kazakhstan and delivers roughly 200,000 b/d to Xinjiang. Existing Russian and Kazakhstani overland pipelines have delivery capacity of about 1.2 MMbpd; in a crisis, China would likely be able to access these full volumes, albeit at a possible premium.
Tier 2B consists of Russian maritime crude imports. Russia typically ships about 0.75 MMbpd to China from its Kozmino port, near Vladivostok, with other export terminals typically providing about 0.25 MMbpd. The US Navy and coalitional navies would weigh carefully whether to interdict Russian ships and disable Russian exports. Targeting Russian vessels and infrastructure risks horizontal and perhaps even vertical escalation, but in a Taiwan contingency the benefits of disabling Russian energy shipments to the Chinese mainland could, under some conditions, outweigh that risk. To mitigate the risks of maritime transit, Beijing and Moscow might expand the capacity of the mainland China leg of the East Siberia–Pacific Ocean pipeline, “promoting” perhaps 0.8 MMbpd from Tier 2B into Tier 2A.
Tier 3 is the 200,000 b/d pipeline from Myanmar, which delivers oil to Yunnan. This source can be thought of as only quasi-overland, however, as it relies on maritime imports to the Made Island oil import terminal that could be interdicted relatively easily.
Tier 4 imports, meanwhile, consist of all other maritime sources.
China can reliably access about 5.6 MMbpd of crude oil supply from domestic and overland sources if all existing pipeline capacity is utilized. Adding about another 1 MMbpd from Russian maritime imports would bring the total to nearly 6.6 MMbpd. If its most secure supplies are operable in a crisis, then about 30 percent of China’s supplies would hinge on Russia, demonstrating Beijing’s interest in maintaining close ties with Moscow.
Turning to demand, China’s refinery runs for crude oil stood at about 15.2 MMbpd in January–February 2026 (assuming 7.33 barrels/ton). Amid the US–Iran war, these runs fell to about 12.5 MMbpd in June, per China’s National Bureau of Statistics. In a contingency, Beijing could again sharply reduce its demand, including in petrochemicals, which accounts for about 25 percent of Chinese oil demand and largely serves the export market. In addition, Beijing could order refineries to maximize output of transportation fuels, including diesel and jet fuel for its military.
Given that total domestic supply from production and secure import capacity equals 6.6 MMbpd, and assuming total refinery runs of 12.5 MMbpd seen in June 2026, China would face a daily deficit of about 5.9 MMbpd in a contingency today. Assuming that China has reserves of about 1.1 billion barrels of crude oil after Iran war-related drawdowns, and that it would be able to draw inventories to only 20 percent before facing constraints from geographic dispersion and tank draw, China would be able to sustain at least one hundred and fifty days of civilian and military activities before reaching physical shortage.
By 2030, however, Beijing will very likely enjoy far greater oil security. Tier 1 and 2A overland crude supplies could very easily rise to 6.8 MMbpd on higher domestic production and greater overland tie-ins with Russian and Central Asian crude oil pipelines. Crude oil demand, meanwhile, could fall to 11.5 MMbpd amid vehicle electrification, leaving a deficit of 4.7 MMbpd. Assuming 1.2 billion barrels of crude oil reserves and a maximum drawdown of inventories to 20 percent, Beijing could likely cover at least two hundred days of refinery runs in a contingency by 2030. Beijing may soon be able to withstand an oil blockade for well over half a year, and perhaps much longer if it continues to increase the size of its oil reserves, can still access Russian maritime imports, or accelerates vehicle electrification.
The United States’ implicit answer to a potential Taiwan quarantine has been to impose a counter-blockade of China’s oil imports. That strategy is increasingly outdated. Policymakers in Washington, Taipei, Tokyo, and beyond need to understand this dangerous new reality, insulate against an energy quarantine, and find other sources of coercive leverage against Beijing.
Taiwan’s exposure: Two likely scenarios for an energy quarantine
Taiwan’s indigenous energy production (including nuclear energy generation) as a percentage of all energy demand declined from 8.3 percent to 5.3 percent from 2016 to 2025.
Taiwan’s reserves of oil, coal, and LNG are required to cover ninety days, thirty days, and eleven days of consumption for each commodity, respectively, although inventories typically cover more. In March 2026, the Ministry of Economic Affairs reported oil, coal, and LNG on-hand inventories of one hundred and fifty days, forty days, and eleven days, respectively. Still, Taiwan’s actual days of consumption covered vary based on several factors, including seasonal weather patterns, its ability to export goods such as semiconductors from its energy-intensive industrial sector, and the continued operation of refineries.
Other regional democracies’ roles in a Taiwan contingency could be constrained by their energy-related vulnerabilities. Japan and South Korea also have limited storage inventories, while other US allies such as the Philippines and Australia are themselves highly reliant on energy imports. Australia’s fuel dependency is staggering: it relies on imports for 83 percent of all refined petroleum products. The coalition has serious work to do to improve its collective energy resilience, and to do so quickly.
If Beijing attempted to subjugate Taiwan via an energy quarantine, two scenarios are most likely. Beijing might straightforwardly implement a quarantine or even blockade of Taiwan, attempting to interdict any inbound energy shipments via its coast guard by claiming a legal pretext.
Alternatively, Beijing might try an indirect approach by exploiting or even stimulating a future Middle Eastern oil crisis. Surging oil prices would disproportionately damage Beijing’s regional rivals, which are relatively reliant on oil imports even as China increasingly turns into a self-sufficient electrotech state.
Timing the risk: Quarantine dangers might peak in 2028 and 2029
The dangers of an energy-weighted geopolitical crisis over Taiwan are already serious but might peak in 2028 and 2029 due to economics, politics, Taiwan’s electricity reserve margins, military readiness, and AI. Mainland China’s economy is showing significant strain even as Taiwan’s powers ahead; both Taiwan and the United States will hold key elections in 2028; Taiwan’s electricity reserve margin is on track to reach dangerously low levels in this period; US military readiness levels might be damaged by protracted deployments in other theaters; and while AI timelines are highly unpredictable, the United States might begin to experience takeoff growth, which could enable it to establish permanent technological dominance. Given these factors, and his own age, Xi might believe by 2028 that he has a limited window of opportunity to act.
Beijing has economic reasons for attempting to control Taiwan sooner rather than later. If economic trends continue, Beijing’s comparative performance legitimacy will weaken vis-à-vis Taiwan through January 2028. Taiwan’s gross domestic product (GDP) growth is projected to reach an astonishing 11 percent in 2026. While most economic growth is concentrated in the tech sector, real median incomes are rising, Taiwan’s government is flush enough to disburse cash payments, the fiscal budget is balanced, and Taiwan’s debt-to-GDP ratio is the lowest in East Asia. Taiwan’s economy is doing well, even if growth will likely decelerate.
Conversely, while Beijing retains formidable economic power, mainland China’seconomy shows significant weakness. Growth rates are undeniably slowing. Chinese debt levels are in a “league of their own,” according to Mark Williams, chief Asia economist at Capital Economics. Logan Wright, partner at Rhodium Group, warns that Beijing’s growth model is “fundamentally broken” and faces “steady decay.” The risks to mainland China’s economy may provide added urgency for Xi to pursue an energy quarantine of Taiwan and coerce it into accepting Beijing’s rule. Assuming current economic trends continue, Taiwan’s living standards will further outpace mainland China’s, significantly damaging the appeal of unification for Taiwan’s voters.
Taiwan will hold its next presidential election in January 2028. While nothing is certain, the outcome of the election is likely to lead to intense discomfort in Beijing (as the author has been warning since June 2026). In most democracies, rising living standards benefit the incumbent party. That means that the Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) is likely to prevail in 2028 presidential elections, assuming Taiwan maintains robust economic growth, which is likely; the DPP is also favored to obtain a majority in the Legislative Yuan, Taiwan’s parliament. Living standards are not the only variable affecting elections, and the composition of candidates from the three main parties in Taiwan will matter greatly for the 2028 election, governing, and cross-Strait relations. Nonetheless, initial indications suggest that political economy trends in Taiwan do not appear to be moving in Beijing’s favor.
As political economy theory might predict, Taiwan’s voters may be rewarding the incumbent party for producing rising living standards. In a stunning reversal from even a few months ago, the DPP is now favored to win the Taipei mayoral race. The approval rating of President Lai Ching-te of the DPP has steadily climbed for months and is at its highest level since April 2025. Other parties could still win in 2028, especially if economic growth falters, perhaps due to an AI market correction in the United States. Nonetheless, assuming robust (and reasonably well-distributed) economic growth continues, then the DPP will likely win both the presidential and the Legislative Yuan elections in January 2028, to Beijing’s immense dissatisfaction.
The United States will also hold its own presidential election in November 2028. Political trends indicate the election will be divisive, potentially distracting Americans from cross-Strait affairs. In addition, while Beijing eyes Trump warily, CCP leaders believe Trump’s transactional approach to governing might offer opportunities vis-à-vis Taiwan in the remainder of his term.
Technical factors will amplify political and economic risks. Taipower, Taiwan’s state-run power company, projects that its nighttime reserve margin will fall to about 8 percent in 2028 and 2029, far below its targeted reserve margin of 15 percent. If current trends continue, Taiwan’s power sector could face interrupted power supplies at night even in peacetime, which would make it even more vulnerable to a potential energy quarantine.
Beijing will also be weighing US military readiness and weapons inventory levels. Where these will stand in 2028 is uncertain, especially if the US conflict in Iran escalates.
AI timelines are their own huge source of uncertainty for 2028–2029. Beijing’s perception that the United States might be on the verge of establishing permanent technological dominance via powerful AI might upend Xi’s assumptions about the desirability of strategic patience and further incentivize Xi to intervene against Taiwan, the world’s most advanced chipmaker.
Finally, there is the human element: Xi’s own sense of destiny. If Taiwan shows no medium-term interest in peacefully or semi-peacefully uniting with the mainland, then Xi might feel pressure to act. He will turn seventy-five in 2028, will have limited patience for sentiment to change through future Taiwanese elections in 2032 or even 2036, and has made clear he does not want the Taiwan issue ‘passed down from generation to generation.’
All these considerations do not guarantee that 2028–2029 will be the peak period of risks in US-China relations. Risks might persist for decades. Still, these factors suggest a convergence of serious, compounding risks that warrant preparation and mitigation.
A strategy for deterrence: Taiwan and its friends should prepare for an energy contingency
There is a need to hedge against the foreseeable and highly consequential risk of an energy quarantine of Taiwan by Beijing, perhaps as early as 2028. While Taiwan is already taking important steps to enhance its energy resilience, its government and the United States must do more to prepare for this risk—and quickly.
To address its urgent energy security challenges, Taiwan needs to take an all-of-the-above approach to electricity generation while bolstering transmission.
Nuclear energy, in particular, is one of the most important pillars of Taiwan’s energy resiliency and should be expanded. Nuclear energy can operate continuously for at least eighteen months once fueled. Additionally, reactors are unlikely to be deliberately destroyed by CCP forces in a contingency. Beijing does not want to risk radiation exposure on the island it seeks to seize. Working with the United States, Japan, and other actors, Taiwan should seek to expand nuclear energy capacity as quickly as possible and start bringing its third nuclear power plant in Maanshan back online in 2028.
In addition to nuclear energy, Taiwan should expand use of LNG, renewables, oil for generation and transportation, and even coal where appropriate. Taiwan should continue to deepen ties with the US LNG complex; expanding natural gas storage capacity will also prove useful.
Finally, and most importantly, the island should adopt a “north diesel, south renewables” approach to electricity generation in preparation for a contingency, and resource this plan effectively.
Northern Taiwan, home to the capital Taipei, is critical. While northern Taiwan has some limited generation capacity, it is a net “importer” from the southern and central parts of the island, in what officials call ”南電北送,”or “send southern power north.” In a contingency, northern Taiwan might not be able to access power generation from the southern and central regions due to sabotage of power stations, substations, transmission lines, or other infrastructure. Moreover, northern Taiwan cannot rely on local renewables generation: Taipei’s solar capacity factor is, inadequately, about the same as Seattle’s, onshore land availability to build more solar is minimal, and regional offshore wind projects, while useful, generate less power in peak summer electricity demand months and also face sabotage risks. Finally, gas-fired power plants at Datan and Tunghsiao constitute the bulk of northern Taiwan’s indigenous power generation, and northern Taiwan’s LNG inventories are finite. If south-to-north transmission lines are cut in a contingency, Taipei could run out of electricity in under one month.
Fuels, especially diesel, are therefore critical for countering an energy quarantine or blockade of Taiwan, particularly one that could occur on a short timeline before the island has time to strengthen resilience through nuclear energy expansion and other tactics. Diesel can be stored for long periods of time and can provide distributed power without transmission wires, as Ukraine is proving. Additionally, diesel units can be deployed in a matter of weeks, although deploying this systematically will require more time and resources.
For approximately $10 billion in up-front capital expenditure plus an estimated $500 million a year to maintain, test, and rotate fuel, northern Taiwan could field about 2 gigawatts of diesel generation (based on author calculations). About half of the capital expenditures would be for a dedicated diesel fuel stockpile and dispersed, hardened storage; generators would account for the rest of the initial outlay. That level of diesel generation would provide enough power to keep hospitals, cooling stations, sanitation, telecom, and emergency services running in northern Taiwan for roughly five months without any power from the south. Taiwan could very likely stand up a first tranche of this system by summer 2027, when it could conduct power generation exercises as part of the Urban Resilience drills. The full buildout could be completed across 2028 and 2029 (and accelerated as needed).
In addition, Taiwan’s southern and central regions have large existing thermal generation power plants along with good-to-excellent renewable resources that cannot be interdicted easily, as they are less reliant on vulnerable, long-distance transmission lines and infrastructure that carry power north. In addition to strengthening the resilience of thermal power plants, including by stockpiling coal and natural gas reserves, Taiwan should increase construction of onshore solar and wind resources in the southern and central regions. Distributed renewables generation is much more difficult to take offline by Chinese forces in a quarantine, blockade, siege, or invasion.
With diesel generation in the north, generation from coal, gas, and nuclear power plants in the south, distributed renewables throughout the island, and aggressive rationing, Taiwan could extend its ability to endure an energy blockade from mere weeks to months.
Taiwan need not act alone, however. The United States has a critical role to play in averting a Taiwan energy contingency. US firms should engage with counterparts in Taiwan across all parts of the energy supply chain, including diesel generators and storage, LNG infrastructure, nuclear energy know-how, and solar and energy storage systems. The chief US contribution to Taiwan’s energy infrastructure might be preventing sabotage. In a contingency, CCP intelligence services would likely seek to degrade or disable Taiwan’s south-to-north power transmission lines and other energy infrastructure with either cyber or kinetic means. To accomplish kinetic sabotage, CCP intelligence services would use the full spectrum of their assets, including their connections with criminal networks. Accordingly, the United States should rotate a far greater number of energy, counternarcotics, and countersabotage personnel through Taiwan, drawing on the Department of Energy, the Drug Enforcement Administration, the Federal Bureau of Investigation, and other civilian security agencies, through the American Institute in Taiwan.
China’s vulnerabilities: Leverage that could enforce stability
In addition to precautionary defensive measures, Washington, Taipei, and other actors should find other forms of leverage over Beijing. China’s food vulnerabilities are significant, while its steel industry relies extensively on Australian iron ore imports. Analysts should carefully scrutinize these commodities, especially if China begins to build inventories.
The most effective form of leverage vis-à-vis Beijing, however, could be economic and financial. China’s economic growth model might be broken. China remains highly reliant on other countries absorbing its overcapacity, as net exports’ contribution to GDP growth stood at 32.7 percent, the highest level since 1997. Far from successfully rebalancing, China’s economic and financial model has become more reliant on exports, investments, and debt, raising the likelihood of a painful correction. If Beijing attempted to coerce Taiwan, including through an energy quarantine, China’s ability to reach export markets might be imperiled due to a combination of economic, financial, cyber, and other measures. If China loses substantial access to export markets due to an unwise attempt to coerce Taipei, the risks for its economic, financial, social, and ultimately political stability could be profound.
While the risks of an energy quarantine are significant and rising, Taipei and Washington are well positioned to mitigate these dangers. Taiwan is already making great strides in enhancing its energy resilience. It should build on these efforts by building new generation for the long term and, especially, leveraging diesel as a near-term bridge solution. Similarly, Washington should take a more active role in opposing unilateral changes to the status quo by either side. Washington should underscore its continued commitment to the “One China” policy, anchored to the Taiwan Relations Act, the three communiqués, and the Six Assurances, while warning Beijing not to undertake aggression. If Taipei and Washington can see through this moment of danger, they could settle into a period of relative stability.
Joseph Webster is a nonresident senior fellow at the Atlantic Council’s Global Energy Center and the Indo-Pacific Security Initiative; he also edits the independent China-Russia Report. This analysis reflects his personal opinion.

content:
如果黑客能夠控制超市的冷凍櫃，其他科技設備又有多脆弱？ - BBC News 中文
Author, 希奧娜·麥卡勒姆（Shiona McCallum）
歐洲多地超市近日遭遇一起疑似網絡攻擊，影響其冷藏櫃和冷凍櫃，並引發外界對互聯網連接硬件漏洞的憂慮。這些硬件涵蓋工業機械，以至日常家用電器。
連接互聯網的智能設備可以包括冰箱、中央供暖系統，甚至洗衣機。
雖然這類設備因此更容易被遠程控制，但理論上，任何接入網絡的設備都有可能被惡意行為者利用。
然而，這並不意味著黑客能輕易取得控制權，而且大型品牌通常會投入大量資源，確保其產品的安全性。
過去曾在部分設備中發現漏洞。2015年，研究人員展示了三星（Samsung）智能冰箱中的一項漏洞，如何讓他們攔截互聯網流量。
不過，目前沒有證據顯示，在11月針對超市發動的網絡攻擊中，家用電器成為了攻擊目標。
英國國家網絡安全中心（NCSC）前行政總裁西亞蘭·馬丁（Ciaran Martin）表示，製造商需要採取更多措施，提升連網設備的安全性。
他說：「我們需要對大型科技公司提出更多要求，讓它們從一開始就為我們提供更安全的設備和產品。」
他建議消費者保持設備更新，並在可行情況下啟用多重身份驗證。
自2024年4月起，英國法律已要求部分消費級智能設備製造商符合最低網絡安全標準，包括密碼管理和安全更新方面的要求。
英國國家網絡安全中心表示，正與國際夥伴及業界合作，以了解這些超市事件的情況，但目前並未發現對英國造成任何影響。
不過，英國網絡防禦（UK Cyber Defence）的研究人員已識別出超過800個與英國零售商相關的製冷及樓宇控制系統介面，可透過公共互聯網存取。
這並不一定意味著它們能夠被入侵，但可能使其暴露於利用弱密碼或軟件漏洞的攻擊者面前。
在早前超市遭受網絡攻擊後，政府已與食品零售業高層舉行會談，討論網絡韌性問題。
英國零售聯盟（British Retail Consortium）行政總裁海倫·狄金森（Helen Dickinson）表示，網絡安全事件是零售商的一大憂慮，各企業正與國家網絡安全中心合作，共享情報並強化防禦能力。
2025年5月，英國超市馬莎百貨（M&S）和合作社集團（Co-op）遭勒索軟件黑客攻擊時，兩家零售商一度難以用新鮮貨品補充部分門店貨架。
網絡安全公司 SentinelOne 研究員湯姆·黑格爾（Tom Hegel）表示，零售商必須更清楚界定責任歸屬。
他說：「零售商需要回答的問題是，誰負責這些設備的安全，而不只是誰負責維修它們。」
他表示，互聯網連接能使日常科技產品更加方便，但安全措施必須同步跟上。
他說：「一旦攻擊者能夠操控這些控制系統，像除霜這樣的正常功能也會變成干擾工具。」
他說：「改變一項設定就可能摧毀實體庫存，而不只是干擾電腦系統。」
在家庭以外，連網技術亦被用於遠程管理工業機械和車輛。
網絡安全專家肯·芒羅（Ken Munro）提到2015年的一次演示，研究人員透過一輛Jeep汽車連接互聯網的娛樂系統進行遠程入侵，促使業界加強車輛安全措施。
他說：「幸運的是，汽車行業已意識到這個問題，並作出了修復。」
流動通訊連接也被廣泛用於監察發電廠及供水網絡中的設備，讓工程師能夠遠程管理系統。
芒羅表示，英國公共事業機構在保護這些連接方面普遍做得不錯，但世界各地的標準並不一致。
他最擔心的是規模較小、資金不足的公用事業公司，這些公司可能仍依賴較舊且存在漏洞的設備。
Zscaler 網絡安全專家奧利維耶·達洛伊（Olivier Daloy）表示，如果缺乏適當的保護措施，任何接入互聯網的「工廠或設備」，從汽車製造商到電力或交通基礎設施，都可能面臨類似風險。
本文原以英文撰寫，我們使用了人工智能協助翻譯，並由BBC記者在發佈前進行審核。了解更多關於我們如何使用人工智能的資訊。

summary: 发言人办公室对古巴政权的对外军事支持和非法收入网络的进一步制裁 - 情况说明书 情况说明书 2026 年 11 月 5 日 今天，美国国务院指定了 8 个实体和 2 名个人，并将 5 艘船只确定为封锁财产，以进一步推动特朗普政府全面推动结束古巴政权在古巴和整个半球的恶意活动。这一行动包括与古巴政权的石油运输网络、古巴精英、国有进口和技术支持实体以及中国企业相关的目标。
content:
发言人办公室对古巴政权的对外军事支持和非法收入网络的进一步制裁 - 情况说明书 情况说明书 2026 年 11 月 5 日 今天，美国国务院指定了 8 个实体和 2 名个人，并将 5 艘船只确定为封锁财产，以进一步推动特朗普政府全面推动结束古巴政权在古巴和整个半球的恶意活动。这一行动包括与古巴政权的石油运输网络、古巴精英、国有进口和技术支持实体以及该政权军队的中国供应商相关的目标。今天制裁的所有国务院目标都是根据第 14404 号行政命令 (E.O.) 指定的，该命令授权对符合与古巴镇压以及对美国国家安全和外交政策的其他威胁有关的特定标准的外国人实施制裁。此外，今天，财政部外国资产控制办公室 (OFAC) 主任根据 E.O. 发布了一项决定。第 14404 号法令授权对任何在古巴经济的制造、技术、电子和海洋部门经营或曾经经营的外国人实施制裁。这些新部门的确定针对的是该政权及其支持者，而不是古巴人民。
美国继续授权人道主义贸易，包括食品、药品和医疗设备，并支持信息向古巴人民自由流动。 古巴政权的非法收入网络 古巴的统治精英囤积岛上的能源和航运资源以图谋取私利，使古巴人民面临停电、燃料短缺和经济停滞的困境。为了维持该系统的运行，该政权依赖离岸中介机构网络。今天，美国国务院正在指定为古巴政权运送原油和石油产品的广泛航运网络的一部分。 GUILLERMO FAUSTINO RODRIGUEZ LOPEZ CALLEJA (GUILLERMO) 是往返古巴运输石油产品的广泛海运公司网络的一部分。 GUILLERMO 是根据第 2 节指定的。 E.O. 2(a)(i)(A) 14404 从事或曾经从事古巴经济能源部门的工作。 CAROIL TRANSPORT MARINE LTD (CAROIL) 是一家总部位于塞浦路斯的公司，管理着悬挂古巴国旗的原油油轮，这些油轮在古巴运输能源产品。财政部此前根据 E.O. 于 2019 年 9 月 24 日指定 CAROIL。 13850. CAROIL 根据第 13850 条被指定。 E.O. 2(a)(i)(A) 14404 从事或曾经从事古巴经济能源部门的工作。以下船舶被确定为 CAROIL 拥有权益的财产： ESPERANZA (IMO: 9289166)：CAROIL 是商业管理者。
财政部此前于 2019 年 12 月 3 日将 ESPERANZA 确定为 CAROIL 的冻结财产。 GLORIA C（IMO：9540273）：CAROIL 是商业经理。 TENTACOOL COMMERCIAL INC 是注册所有者。 MARIA CRISTINA（IMO：9502453）：CAROIL 是商业经理和注册所有者。财政部此前于 2019 年 9 月 24 日将 MARIA CRISTINA 确定为 CAROIL 的封锁财产。TENTACOOL COMMERCIAL INC (TENTACOOL) 是一家总部位于巴拿马的公司，也是 GLORIA C 的注册所有者。 E.O. 2(a)(i)(A) 14404 从事或曾经从事古巴经济能源部门的工作。国际会议

Office of the Spokesman Further Sanctions on the Cuban Regime’s Foreign Military Support and Illicit Revenue Networks – Fact Sheet Fact Sheet November 5, 2026 Today, the Department of State is designating eight entities and two individuals, and identifying five vessels as blocked property, to further the Trump Administration’s comprehensive push to end the Cuban regime’s malign activities, both in Cuba and across our hemisphere.  This action includes targets associated with the Cuban regime’s oil shipping networks, Cuban elites, state-owned import and technical-support entities, and China-based suppliers of the regime’s military forces.    All Department of State targets sanctioned today have been designated pursuant to Executive Order (E.O.) 14404, which authorizes sanctions on foreign persons determined to meet specified criteria related to repression in Cuba and other threats to U.S. national security and foreign policy.  Additionally, today the Director of the Department of the Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) issued a determination pursuant to E.O. 14404 that authorizes sanctions against any foreign person operating or having operated in the manufacturing, technology, electronics, and marine sectors of the Cuban economy.  The identification of these new sectors targets the regime and those who enable it, not the Cuban people.  The United States continues to authorize humanitarian trade, including food, medicine, and medical devices, and supports the free flow of information to the Cuban people. Cuban Regime’s Illicit Revenue Networks Cuba’s ruling elite hoards the island’s energy and shipping resources for its own enrichment, leaving the Cuban people to contend with blackouts, fuel shortages, and a stagnant economy. To keep this system running, the regime relies on a web of offshore intermediaries. Today, the Department of State is designating part of an extensive shipping network moving crude oil and petroleum products for the Cuban regime. GUILLERMO FAUSTINO RODRIGUEZ LOPEZ CALLEJA (GUILLERMO) is part of an extensive network of maritime shipping companies moving petroleum products to and from Cuba. GUILLERMO is being designated pursuant to Sec. 2(a)(i)(A) of E.O. 14404 for operating in or having operated in the energy sector of the Cuban economy. CAROIL TRANSPORT MARINE LTD (CAROIL) , a Cyprus-based company that manages Cuban-flagged crude oil tankers that have transported energy products in Cuba. Treasury previously designated CAROIL on September 24, 2019, pursuant to E.O. 13850. CAROIL is being designated pursuant to Sec. 2(a)(i)(A) of E.O. 14404 for operating in or having operated in the energy sector of the Cuban economy. The following vessels are being identified as property in which CAROIL has an interest: ESPERANZA (IMO: 9289166): CAROIL is the commercial manager. Treasury previously identified ESPERANZA as blocked property of CAROIL on December 3, 2019. GLORIA C (IMO: 9540273): CAROIL is the commercial manager. TENTACOOL COMMERCIAL INC, is the registered owner. MARIA CRISTINA (IMO: 9502453): CAROIL is the commercial manager and registered owner. Treasury previously identified MARIA CRISTINA as blocked property of CAROIL on September 24, 2019. TENTACOOL COMMERCIAL INC (TENTACOOL) , a Panama-based company and the registered owner of the GLORIA C. TENTACOOL is being designated pursuant to Sec. 2(a)(i)(A) of E.O. 14404 for operating in or having operated in the energy sector of the Cuban economy. INTERNACIONAL MARITIMA SA , a Cuba-based company and the registered owner of the ESPERANZA. INTERNACIONAL MARITIMA SA is being designated pursuant to Sec. 2(a)(i)(A) of E.O. 14404 for operating in or having operated in the energy sector of the Cuban economy. PETROLEOS MARITIMOS DEL CARIBE S.A. (PETROMARCA) , a Cuba-based company and the ship manager and operator of two Cuban-flagged petroleum product tankers. PETROMARCA is being designated pursuant to Sec. 2(a)(i)(A) of E.O. 14404 for operating in or having operated in the energy sector of the Cuban economy. The following vessels are being identified as property in which PETROMARCA has an interest: EMILIA (IMO: 9242209): PETROMARCA is the commercial manager and registered owner. LOURDES (IMO: 9259692): PETROMARCA is the commercial manager. Cuban Elites Regime insiders and their family members continue to profit from the Cuban regime’s control of the island’s economy, including through opaque networks tied to Grupo De Administracion Empresarial S.A. (GAESA), the Cuban military’s business conglomerate. Today, the Department of State is designating the daughter of the previously designated GAESA President. ANY RODRIGUEZ LASTRES (LASTRES) , the daughter of the sanctioned GAESA President Ania Guillermina Lastres Morera. LASTRES is being designated pursuant to Sec. 2(a)(i)(I) of E.O. 14404 for being an adult family member of ANIA GUILLERMINA LASTRES MORERA, a person whose property and interests in property are blocked pursuant to this order. LASTRES also previously served as the Commercial Director of U.S.-designated Terminal De Contenedores De Mariel S.A. State-Owned Entities of the Cuban Regime The Cuban regime relies on a web of state-owned enterprises that control the island’s technology resources and direct revenue to the state rather than to the Cuban people. Today, the Department of State is designating the following two Cuban state-owned entities pursuant to Sec. 2(a)(i)(B) of E.O. 14404 for being owned, controlled, or directed by, or having acted or purported to act for or on behalf of, directly or indirectly, the Government of Cuba. EMPRESA IMPORTADORA Y EXPORTADORA DE PRODUCTOS DE LA ELECTRONICA Y LAS COMUNICACIONES (CUBAELECTRONICA) , a Cuban state-owned importer of supplies and equipment for Cuba’s electronics industry. EMPRESA COMERCIALIZADORA DE SERVICIOS TECNICOS Y TECNOLOGICOS (TECNOSIME) , a Cuban state-owned entity that conducts commercial, labor, and promotional activities that generate revenue for the Cuban state. Chinese Companies’ Support to the Cuban Military As the Department’s July 20 report Cuba: The Capital of 21st Century Communism noted, the Cuban regime’s continuing partnerships with China and Russia have supplied Cuba with military hardware, surveillance technologies, and other security capabilities. Today, the Department of State is taking aim at Cuba’s foreign backers by designating two China-based corporations that have supplied the Cuban regime with components and equipment to sustain the Cuban military. The transfer of this equipment involved the Cuban company Sociedad Mercantil Duna S.A., which was designated by the Department of State on August 6, 2026 , and has been involved in the import of military-related equipment from China and Russia to Cuba. The following entities are being designated pursuant to Sec. 2(a)(i)(D) of E.O. 14404 for having materially assisted, sponsored, or provided financial, material, or technological support for, or goods or services to or in support of, the Government of Cuba. CHINA NATIONAL ELECTRONIC IMPORT AND EXPORT COMPANY (CEIEC) , a China-based state-owned enterprise that exports defense electronics, security systems, and construction engineering services. Additionally, CEIEC contracted with the Cuban arms procurement entity Sociedad Mercantil Duna S.A. to export components intended for military equipment used by the Cuban Ministry of Revolutionary Armed Forces (MINFAR) in 2026. CEIEC was previously designated by the Department of the Treasury pursuant to E.O. 13692 on November 30, 2020 , in relation to its support for the Maduro regime’s efforts to restrict internet service and conduct digital surveillance and cyber operations against political opponents. BEIJING H&C TECHNOLOGIES CO., LTD , a China-based subsidiary of China Electronics Technology Group Corporation (CETC) International Co., Ltd. (CETCI) that sells surveillance and security equipment. Additionally, BEIJING H&C TECHNOLOGIES CO., LTD worked with the Cuban arms procurement entity Sociedad Mercantil Duna S.A. to export military equipment to Cuba in 2026. Sanctions Implications As a result of today’s sanctions actions, and in accordance with E.O. 14404 of May 1, 2026, “Imposing Sanctions on Those Responsible for Repression in Cuba and for Threats to U.S. National Security and Foreign Policy,” all property and interests in property of the designated persons described above that are in the United States or in possession or control of U.S. persons are blocked and must be reported to OFAC. Additionally, all entities that are owned individually or in the aggregate, 50 percent or more by one or more blocked persons are also blocked. All transactions and dealings by U.S. persons or persons within (or transiting) the United States that involve any property or interests in property of designated or otherwise blocked persons are prohibited unless authorized by a general or specific license issued by OFAC or exempt. These prohibitions include the making of any contribution or provision of funds, goods, or services by, to, or for the benefit of any blocked person and the receipt of any contribution or provision of funds, goods, or services from any such person. Foreign persons that engage in transactions with persons designated pursuant to E.O. 14404—or that operate or have operated in the electronics, energy, defense and related materiel, manufacturing, marine, metals and mining, financial services, security, or technology sector of the Cuban economy, as identified in and determined pursuant to E.O. 14404—are themselves at risk of sanctions.  Non-U.S. persons, including foreign financial institutions, should proceed with caution in any dealings with a party sanctioned under this authority. Actions to return assets to a sanctioned party or transfer them to another jurisdiction for potential use by the target expose non-U.S. persons to significant sanctions risk. All property and interests in property of persons that are blocked pursuant to the Cuban Assets Control Regulations (CACR) continue to be blocked.  The CACR prohibits persons subject to U.S. jurisdiction from dealing in property in which Cuba or a Cuban national has an interest, unless authorized or exempt.  The power and integrity of U.S. government sanctions derive not only from the U.S. government’s ability to designate and add persons to the Specially Designated Nationals and Blocked Persons (SDN) List, but also from its willingness to remove persons from the SDN List consistent with the law. The ultimate goal of sanctions is not to punish, but to bring about a positive change in behavior.    Petitions for removal from the SDN List may be routed through OFAC’s Reconsiderations Portal . Petitioners may also refer to the Department of State’s Delisting Guidance page.

title: The Pentagon needs more ammo for the Iran war. Small communities are paying the price.
zh_title: 五角大楼需要更多弹药来应对伊朗战争。小社区正在付出代价。
summary: 编者注：本文首次发表于《战马》，这是一家屡获殊荣的非营利新闻机构，旨在教育公众服兵役。订阅他们的时事通讯。 2024 年秋天，飓风海伦席卷东海岸，新河的水淹没了城镇，摧毁了西弗吉尼亚州、北卡罗来纳州和弗吉尼亚州部分地区的桥梁。在弗吉尼亚州雷德福，洪水最高达到 31 英尺。就在下游，河水涌入雷德福德陆军弹药厂，冲破了仓库大门，冲毁了十几个装有数千名弹药的储存容器。
content:
编者注：本文首次发表于《战马》，这是一家屡获殊荣的非营利新闻机构，旨在教育公众服兵役。订阅他们的时事通讯。 2024 年秋天，飓风海伦席卷东海岸，新河的水淹没了城镇，摧毁了西弗吉尼亚州、北卡罗来纳州和弗吉尼亚州部分地区的桥梁。在弗吉尼亚州雷德福，洪水最高达到 31 英尺。就在下游，河流涌入雷德福德陆军弹药厂，冲破仓库大门，冲走了十几个装有数千加仑有毒化学品的储存容器。直到几周后，陆军才向居民发出关于装满邻苯二甲酸二丁酯的集装箱的警告，邻苯二甲酸二丁酯是火箭推进剂的关键成分，与人类癌症和生殖问题有关，还有数百加仑柴油和超过10万磅被硫酸钙污染的废水，这些集装箱已在洪水中被冲走。官员们后来表示，他们假设这些集装箱会沉入河底，洪水会稀释任何化学品泄漏。然而，至少有一个集装箱被冲到附近的土地上，部分集装箱已被排干。据弗吉尼亚州环境质量部称，两年后，三人仍下落不明，该部门发现超过 1,500 加仑的液体已泄漏到环境中。
雷德福陆军弹药厂早在 2024 年就因向新河排放超标污染物而被点名。它在 2023 年也面临着类似的处罚。2022 年，弗吉尼亚州环境监管机构将雷德福列为该州最大的毒素排放者。 “他们经常被指责向水中添加过量的铅，或向空气中释放其他有毒物质，或者燃烧比预期更多的化学物质，”阿森纳责任公民组织的创始人艾莉莎·卡彭特说，该组织倡导在雷德福德采取更严格的环保措施。雷德福德也是国家军火供应链的重要组成部分：它是火炮和火箭所用某些类型推进剂的唯一国内生产商。当五角大楼采取行动补充其耗尽的弹药库存并增加产量时，它在一定程度上依赖于雷德福等老化的陆军弹药工厂网络，其中一些工厂有着长期违反环境和安全法规的历史。一名工人在雷德福陆军弹药厂检查火箭筒推进剂。 （多丽丝·惠普尔摄，雷德福德陆军弹药厂提供）支持者表示，军方经常将这些风险视为生产的次要风险，让工人和附近社区承担后果。
“国防部机构的记录并不好，”在奥巴马政府期间帮助监督环境保护局有毒物质清理工作的马西·斯坦尼斯劳斯说，“始终是防御。‘这是我们的使命。’其他一切都是次要的。”现在，支持者担心生产更多弹药的压力可能会加剧当地社区面临的风险。他们认为，重建美国军火库的成本不成比例地由工厂工人和设施周围的大多数农村社区承担。卡彭特说：“这对军队来说很便宜，但对我们、对我们的一生来说却非常昂贵。” “如果不增加该产品产生的有毒副产品，就无法增加产量

Editor’s note: This article first appeared on The War Horse , an award-winning nonprofit news organization educating the public on military service. Subscribe to their newsletter . When Hurricane Helene ripped up the East Coast in the fall of 2024, water from the New River flooded towns and destroyed bridges across parts of West Virginia, North Carolina, and Virginia. In Radford, Virginia, floodwaters crested at 31 feet. Just downstream, the river surged into the Radford Army Ammunition Plant, tearing through warehouse doors and washing out more than a dozen storage containers with thousands of gallons of toxic chemicals inside. The Army didn’t warn residents until weeks later about the containers filled with dibutyl phthalate, a key component of rocket propellant that has been linked to cancer and reproductive problems in humans — along with hundreds of gallons of diesel fuel and more than 100,000 pounds of wastewater contaminated with calcium sulfate — that had been washed away in the flood. Officials said later that they assumed the containers would sink to the bottom of the river and floodwaters would dilute any chemical leakage. At least one container, however, washed up on nearby land, where it was partially drained. Two years later, three remain unaccounted for, according to the Virginia Department of Environmental Quality, which found that more than 1,500 gallons had leaked into the environment. Radford Army Ammunition Plant had already been cited earlier in 2024 for discharging excessive levels of pollutants into the New River. It faced a similar penalty in 2023. And in 2022, Virginia environmental regulators listed Radford as the state’s top releaser of toxins. “They’re constantly being cited for putting excessive levels of lead into the water, or other toxic releases into the air, or burning more chemicals than they’re supposed to,” said Alyssa Carpenter, a founder of Citizens for Arsenal Accountability, which advocates for stronger environmental practices at Radford. Radford is also a critical part of the nation’s munitions supply chain: It is the only domestic producer of certain types of propellant used in artillery and rockets. As the Pentagon moves to replenish its depleted munitions stockpile and increase production, it is relying in part on a network of aging Army ammunition plants like Radford, several of which have long histories of violating environmental and safety regulations. A worker inspects rocket tube propellant at Radford Army Ammunition Plant. (Photo by Doris Whipple, courtesy of Radford Army Ammunition Plant) Advocates say the military has too often treated those risks as secondary to production, leaving workers and nearby communities to absorb the consequences. “The track record of the Department of Defense agencies is not good,” said Mathy Stanislaus, who helped oversee toxic cleanup efforts at the Environmental Protection Agency during the Obama administration. “It’s always defense. ‘That’s our mission.’ Everything else is secondary.” Now, advocates worry that pressure to produce more ammunition could intensify the risk to local communities. They argue that the costs of rebuilding America’s arsenal are being borne disproportionately by plant workers and the mostly rural communities surrounding the facilities. “It’s cheap for the military, but it is very expensive for us, for our entire lives,” Carpenter said. “You can’t increase production without increasing the toxic byproducts that come from that production.” An Aging Arsenal As the United States entered World War II, the Army built a network of ammunition plants across the country that became part of Franklin Roosevelt’s “arsenal of democracy.” Many were decommissioned after the war and more closed by the end of the Cold War. Today, much of the defense industrial base is run by private companies, but the Army still manages a network of specialized arsenals, ammunition plants, and maintenance depots, many of which help manufacture, test, and repair missiles, heavy ordnance, and their components, handling work that ranges from creating raw explosive chemicals and rocket propellant to loading warheads and artillery shells. The United States military is running low on several critical munitions. A report from the Center for Strategic and International Studies published this summer estimated that U.S. inventory of Patriot interceptor missiles had fallen from more than 2,300 at the start of the Iran War to around 800 by the end of July. Stocks of THAAD interceptors, which shoot down incoming ballistic missiles, had likewise fallen by nearly half, from roughly 450 before the war. Stocks of THAAD interceptors have reportedly declined by nearly half since the start of the Iran War. (Missile Defense Agency) The strain predates the Iran War, however. U.S. inventories of precision-guided weapons and heavy conventional ordnance stockpiles had already been under pressure from decades of post-Cold War factory consolidation and shipments to allies overseas. Before Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, the United States produced about 14,000 155 mm artillery shells a month. At times, Ukrainian soldiers were burning through that many rounds in just a few days. And historically, munitions production has often lost out to other priorities in Pentagon budget fights. “When you’re putting together a budget, you can’t just ask for everything,” said Carlton Haelig, who works on defense strategy at the Center for a New American Security. “When there need to be cuts to pay for an extra squadron [of fighter jets] purchased, another set of transport aircraft, surface ships, whatever, the place that is often considered for making those cuts is in the munitions portfolio.” In recent years, however, concern about a potential confrontation with China has pushed the Pentagon to expand munitions production. Last year, the Defense Department established a new council tasked with dramatically increasing production of 14 weapons systems, and it has poured billions of dollars toward accelerating production of 155 mm artillery shells. Environmental advocates worry that pushing more production through aging Army facilities could worsen existing problems with pollution, worker safety, and transparency. “Measured by the number of sites where hazardous substances have been released into the environment, the military is far and away the largest polluter in the United States,” said Lenny Siegel, an expert on military contamination who leads the Center for Public Environmental Oversight. “I see the simple issue of math. If you’re releasing X into the environment now, you’re going to release 10X when you multiply your production by 10.” Justine Barati, a spokesperson for the Army Sustainment Command, which oversees these facilities, disagreed. “The U.S. Army does not, and will never, compromise the safety of our workforce or our surrounding communities to meet production quotas. Protecting our people and the environment is foundational to national security,” she said. “We cannot sustain warfighter readiness without safe, resilient, and compliant installations.” Barati pointed to a sweeping $18 billion modernization effort across these facilities, saying the Army’s “highest priority” in the modernization is to improve environmental compliance and workplace safety. But that project is not scheduled to be completed until 2038, and the Army is already accelerating production at some facilities. “At the same time, the Ukraine war started to get hot and heavy, and we were given the edict that’s like, ‘hurry up and go fast’,” Maj. Gen. John Reim, head of the joint armaments and ammunitions program executive office, told Breaking Defense last year. Marines load an M777 towed 155 mm howitzer into the cargo hold of a plane to send in support of Ukraine’s efforts against the Russian invasion. (Cpl. Austin Fraley/U.S. Marine Corps) EPA records show that all the Army ammunition plants and arsenals involved in producing, testing, or storing weapon components have been cited or flagged for noncompliance by the EPA or state regulators in the past five years. Four of them have been flagged for “significant noncompliance” by the EPA, designating them severe or chronic violators of environmental law. Many of them have also violated state environmental regulations. EPA records show Scranton Army Ammunition Plant in Pennsylvania, for instance, which helps forge steel 155 mm shell bodies, was flagged for violating the Clean Water Act and Clean Air Act multiple times during 2024 and 2025. At the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in 2023, regulators found workers improperly detonated explosives in a detonation chamber, among other issues. At Holston Army Ammunition Plant in Kingsport, Tennessee, BAE Systems, which operates the plant, was fined this October by the Tennessee Department of Environment and Conservation’s air pollution control division for improper record-keeping and reporting of data. Federal and state regulators can inspect and penalize these facilities, but the fines are often small compared with the sheer size and resources of the Defense Department. After EPA inspectors found alleged violations at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant, in 2024, the EPA fined the Army and plant operator American Ordnance just under $40,000 — compare that with a $53 million Army contract American Ordnance was awarded this year for its work at the plant. “The biggest problem is that the Department of Defense is effectively self-regulating,” Stanislaus, the former EPA official, said. “When the rubber hits the road, EPA and state agencies simply do not have the authority to mandate certain activities, everything from preventing harm to doing the cleanup.” A Whistleblower’s Safety Concerns The fire that erupted on a July night in Crane, Indiana, burned for 15 hours. Workers at Crane Army Ammunition Activity, which disposes of old munitions, had been storing mortar rounds outdoors in wooden crates beneath a tarp in the baking sun. Temperatures had climbed into the high 90s for several days. The rounds contained red phosphorus, which can generate heat and flammable gases as it degrades. On the evening of July 6, 2022, nearly 115,000 pounds of red phosphorus ignited, sending flames and smoke billowing into the sky. A fire resulting from improperly stored mortar rounds erupted at Naval Weapons Station Crane in 2022. (Photo courtesy of Rick Ward) What happened before and after illustrates how difficult it can be to hold these facilities accountable. Three years earlier, Rick Ward, the newly hired safety chief at Crane Army Ammunition Activity, which is housed at Naval Weapons Station Crane, had concerns with safety at the facility. A safety program for controlling hazardous substances was not fully implemented. Hazardous processes weren’t properly classified. Slings used to move heavy explosives didn’t have current certifications. Ward pointed to an earlier explosion at Crane, in 2013, that sent five people to the hospital. An OSHA inspection afterward identified three dozen safety violations, and an Army “lessons learned” report cited a lack of clear safety procedures. Ward worried that the safety culture at Crane hadn’t changed. He began bringing concerns up with his supervisors, according to documents he shared with The War Horse. “Can you imagine taking over as a safety director and knowing that you’ve been handed 36 OSHA violations that never got corrected?” he said. The year before Ward arrived, EPA had also cited Naval Weapons Station Crane — the base where Crane Army Ammunition Activity is housed — for improperly storing hazardous waste. But Ward felt his concerns were not being taken seriously. So in 2020, he filed an anonymous complaint with OSHA. Rick Ward, the former civilian safety chief at Crane Army Ammunition Activity, was fired after he brought up safety concerns. (Photo courtesy of Rick Ward) Because of COVID-related restrictions, OSHA asked the Army to investigate the allegations itself. Ironically, Crane leaders assigned Ward to conduct the investigation. About an hour after Ward submitted his report, he said, he was put on administrative leave. He was fired several months later, according to a statement from his lawyers. Ward has struggled to find work ever since. Crane barred him from the installation, and the Air Force, where he serves as a reserve officer, revoked his security clearance. “It’s really hard to get a job when you’ve been on the front page of every newspaper in Indiana,” he said. Barati, the Army Sustainment Command spokesperson, disputed Ward’s account. “The Army did not retaliate against Mr. Rick Ward in any form or manner. The Army takes workplace safety very seriously and welcomes safety concern feedback from all our employees,” she said. Many of Ward’s concerns were later substantiated. A whistleblower investigation partially or fully upheld five of his eight allegations. Among them: Crane did not maintain an accurate list of locations where hazardous work occurred and lacked a complete safety plan for controlling and handling hazardous substances. EPA inspections in 2023 and 2024 found additional problems at Naval Weapons Station Crane. Inspectors reported materials were still stored in ways that could create fire risks, hazardous materials lacked proper labeling, open containers held corrosive waste, and hazardous waste was kept onsite for more than three times the legal time limit. “If you mislabel a particular compound, and you put it into a vessel that cannot handle the corrosiveness of that, then it leaks through that vessel and contaminates the ground,” Stanislaus said. “Terrible things can happen.” Last fall, EPA notified Naval Weapons Station Crane that it planned to assess nearly $250,000 in penalties for the violations. That is a significant EPA penalty. But for Crane, it’s barely a line item in the budget. Toxins in the Air Not long after Alyssa Carpenter graduated from Virginia Tech in 2017, just a few miles from the Radford Army Ammunition Plant, she had to have her thyroid removed. She was 26, otherwise healthy, and had no family history of thyroid cancer. Doctors told her the gland was covered in suspicious nodules. Carpenter cannot say for sure what caused her condition. But as a student at Virginia Tech, she had advocated for better environmental controls at the plant, and she worries the chemicals the plant releases into the environment may have played a role in her illness. Alyssa Carpenter worries her thyroid condition is linked to toxic chemicals from Radford Army Ammunition Plant. (Photo courtesy of Alyssa Carpenter) For decades, Radford and other military facilities have disposed of old munitions and production waste by burning or detonating them in the open, releasing toxic gases, particulate matter, and volatile organic compounds into the air. The United States generally banned open burning and open detonation of hazardous waste in 1980 but created an exception for explosive waste that could not safely be treated another way. That exception has allowed the practice to continue at military and civilian munition facilities. In 2025, 45 years after the ban, 64 public and private facilities across the United States were still allowed to burn or detonate hazardous waste. Residents around Radford have long raised concerns about thyroid disease in the area, though a 2022 review of cancer-registry data by VPM News , a local NPR station, found mixed evidence of unusually high rates. What is clear is that the plant regularly releases hazardous pollutants into the air. According to EPA data, in 2024, Radford released into the air — along with other chemicals — 19,000 pounds of ammonia, which reacts with the atmosphere to create a fine particulate matter known to cause respiratory distress, and more than 900 pounds of lead compounds or lead, a neurotoxin with no known safe level of human exposure. EPA requires facilities to report lead emissions if they exceed just 100 pounds a year. Barati, the Army Sustainment Command spokesperson, said that Radford had reduced the amount of waste treated by open burning by more than 50% since 2017. She also pointed to a new energetic waste incinerator under construction at the facility that will ultimately replace the need for open burning. The incinerator, originally scheduled to be completed in 2025 , will not be operational until 2027, Barati said. Open burns are subject to environmental limits, and facilities are supposed to account for wind patterns and other factors to make burns safer. But those safeguards can be difficult to enforce. At Crane, for instance, EPA inspectors cited the facility in 2023 for conducting burns when its own records showed weather conditions outside permitted limits. (Crane officials told the EPA weather was recorded at a different time of day and that the weather was in parameters when it conducted the burns). Technology has changed since the U.S. allowed an exception for the open burning or detonation of military munitions in 1980. Many other countries, including Germany and Canada, have banned open burning and open detonation of hazardous waste, and military munitions are disposed of in contained burn chambers or closed incinerators. In 2024, the EPA proposed new rules that would further restrict the practice and push facilities toward safer alternative technologies. But the rulemaking has stalled. An EPA spokesperson told The War Horse that the agency plans to finalize the regulations by the end of this year. A bulldozer shovels refuse in an open air burn pit in Balad, Iraq in 2004. The military moved away from open burning at overseas bases after troops began developing rare cancers and lung conditions. (U.S. Army) The military has moved away from open-air waste burning in recent years at overseas bases. For decades, troops stationed in Iraq, Afghanistan, and other countries burned everything from medical waste and plastics to old explosives in open burn pits. Military officials defended the pits as a practical necessity in remote war zones. Like the residents of some communities near ammunition plants in the U.S., service members at bases with burn pits breathed in toxic air containing particulate matter that irritated their throats and lungs, and heavy metals that accumulated in their tissues. When they came home from deployment, they began developing rare cancers and other diseases. But as veterans reported respiratory illnesses, cancers, and other health problems after breathing in the smoke, public pressure grew. The military eventually curtailed the use of burn pits overseas, and Congress passed the PACT Act in 2022 , expanding VA benefits for millions of veterans exposed to the toxic substances during military service — but there are no such benefits for civilians exposed to domestic burn pits. For Carpenter, that history shows the military can change when the risks become impossible to ignore. “If it’s toxic for service members, then it’s going to be toxic for community members as well,” she said. This article from   The War Horse   was edited by Paul Szoldra, fact-checked by Jess Rohan, and copy-edited by Mitchell Hansen-Dewar.

新加坡——印度[国防部宣布](https://www.pib.gov.in/PressReleasePage.aspx?PRID=2331418&reg=48&lang=2)周一，印度已与两家当地造船厂签署了为其海军建造八艘下一代护卫舰 (NGC) 的合同。

印度政府授予Garden Reach造船与工程有限公司（GRSE）和果阿造船有限公司（GSL）一份价值5386.65亿印度卢比（约合57亿美元）的合同，分别建造五艘和三艘护卫舰。千万是印度计数系统中的一个单位，等于一千万。

据国防部称，这些护卫舰将配备先进的导弹、武器和传感器系统，使舰艇能够应对空中、水面和水下的威胁。
印度国防部在声明中表示：“这些舰艇的入列将显着增强印度海军在保卫海上贸易路线、开展反水面和反潜作战行动、加强海岸防御、开展濒海作战行动以及执行海上存在和监视任务等方面的作战能力。”

印度国防部称此次合同授予是一个“重要的里程碑”，并指出，这标志着印度海军将设计船舶的第一个项目，而政府拥有的造船厂（即国防公共部门事业（DPSU））将在通过竞争过程选择后建造这些船舶。

GRSE 和 GSL 的多数股权均由印度政府持有。

# India taps two domestic shipbuilders for $5.7B corvette program

India awarded Garden Reach Shipbuilders & Engineers and Goa Shipyard Limited contracts to build five and three corvettes, respectively, for the country's navy.

By [Mike Yeo](https://breakingdefense.com/author/myeo/) on November 04, 2026 12:37 pm
