title: How Schools Hid Chinese Communist Party Ties After Hegseth Shut Down 80 Rebranded Confucius Institute Programs
zh_title: 赫格斯关闭 80 个更名的孔子学院项目后，学校如何隐藏与中国共产党的关系
summary: 2017 年 4 月，在德克萨斯州休斯顿举行的第十届全国汉语大会开幕式上，小学生背诵唐诗（618-907）。照片：新华社。战争部长皮特·赫格斯10月23日宣布，五角大楼已关闭30所美国大学的80个项目。这些项目以新名称取代了孔子学院，即中国共产党资助的语言和文化中心，通常保留相同的中国合作伙伴。一些学校和非营利组织隐瞒了这些联系。密歇根大学和亚利桑那州立大学改变了建议
content:
2017 年 4 月，在德克萨斯州休斯顿举行的第十届全国汉语大会开幕式上，小学生背诵唐诗（618-907）。照片：新华社。战争部长皮特·赫格斯10月23日宣布，五角大楼已关闭30所美国大学的80个项目。这些项目以新名称取代了孔子学院，即中国共产党资助的语言和文化中心，通常保留相同的中国合作伙伴。一些学校和非营利组织隐瞒了这些联系。据全国学者协会称，密歇根大学和亚利桑那州立大学更改了记录，使中国的持续资助变得匿名。至少在 2025 年 9 月之前，协调德克萨斯州学校孔子课堂的 ILTexas Global 在网上将自己描述为中国教育部和学区之间的中间人。在华盛顿智库捍卫民主基金会向德克萨斯州公共记录请求索取其孔子课堂文件后，该措辞被删除。根据保卫民主基金会 10 月份的研究，芝加哥公立学校的记录将芝加哥孔子学院列为 2026 财年超过 29 万美元拨款的来源，尽管据报道该学院已于 2020 年关闭。 Jane Lu 同时领导该学院和学区的中文世界语言项目，该项目似乎吸收了该学院 K-12 的工作。
该基金会的报告还提到了文化桥接中心，这是一个向公立学校提供赠款并邀请地区领导人访问中国的非营利组织。该中心主任高青此前曾担任孔子学院美国中心的负责人，该中心被国务院称为孔子学院网络事实上的总部。北京语言大学将该中心列为其全球机构之一，与数十个以孔子名字命名的机构并列。美国第一所孔子学院于 2004 年 11 月与南开大学合作在马里兰大学成立。中国教育部下属的国家汉办提供启动资金、教师和教科书，并将每所主办大学与中国对应大学配对。一份 2019 年参议院两党报告得出的结论是，北京“控制着这些机构的几乎所有方面”，对演讲者和活动使用否决权，以压制校园里对中国的批评。美国官员还指责这些机构散布北京的宣传并为间谍活动和知识产权盗窃提供便利。国会从 2018 年开始限制五角大楼的资助，切断了孔子学院所在大学的中文项目的资金。 2021 财年国防授权法案将限制范围扩大到五角大楼为主办大学提供的所有资助，且没有豁免，无论该项目的名称如何。
到 2023 年底，美国政府问责办公室的统计显示，美国大学的机构数量从大约 100 个减少到不到 5 个。北京在 2020 年重组了该网络。当年 6 月，27 家中国大学、企业和社会组织成立了中国国际教育基金会来管理这些机构。创始人包括北京师范大学、北京语言大学和南开大学。该基金会在中国民政部注册，美国国会研究服务部将其描述为由中国教育部资助的非政府慈善机构

【原文 English Original】
Primary school students recite a Tang Dynasty (618–907) poem at the opening ceremony of the tenth annual National Chinese Language Conference in Houston, Texas, in April 2017. Photo: Xinhua. Secretary of War Pete Hegseth announced Oct. 23 that the Pentagon had shut down 80 programs at 30 American universities. The programs replaced Confucius Institutes , the Chinese Communist Party-funded language and culture centers, under new names, often retaining the same Chinese partners . Some schools and nonprofits concealed those ties. The University of Michigan and Arizona State University altered records to make continued Chinese funding anonymous, according to the National Association of Scholars . Until at least September 2025, ILTexas Global, which coordinated Confucius Classrooms in Texas schools, described itself online as an intermediary between China’s Ministry of Education and school districts. It removed that wording after the Foundation for Defense of Democracies, a Washington think tank, filed a Texas public records request for its Confucius Classroom documents. Chicago Public Schools records list the Confucius Institute of Chicago as the source of more than $290,000 in fiscal 2026 grants, despite its reported closure in 2020, according to the Foundation for Defense of Democracies’ October study. Jane Lu simultaneously headed the institute and the district’s Chinese World Language Program, which appears to have absorbed the institute’s K–12 work. The foundation’s report also identified the Center for Bridging Cultures, a nonprofit that made grants to public schools and invited district leaders on trips to China. Its director, Gao Qing, previously headed the Confucius Institute U.S. Center, which the State Department called the de facto headquarters of the Confucius Institute Network. Beijing Language and Culture University lists the center among its global institutes, alongside dozens that carry the Confucius name. The first U.S. Confucius Institute opened at the University of Maryland in November 2004 in partnership with Nankai University. Hanban, an agency tied to China’s Ministry of Education, supplied start-up funding, instructors and textbooks, and paired each host university with a Chinese counterpart. A bipartisan 2019 Senate report concluded that Beijing “controls nearly every aspect” of the institutes, using veto power over speakers and events to suppress campus criticism of China. U.S. officials also accused the institutes of spreading Beijing’s propaganda and facilitating espionage and intellectual property theft. Congress began restricting Pentagon funding in 2018, cutting off money for Chinese language programs at universities hosting Confucius Institutes. The fiscal 2021 defense authorization act expanded the restriction to all Pentagon funding for host universities without a waiver, regardless of the program’s name. By late 2023, the Government Accountability Office counted fewer than five institutes at U.S. universities, down from about 100. Beijing reorganized the network in 2020. That June, 27 Chinese universities, companies and social organizations founded the Chinese International Education Foundation to oversee the institutes. Founders included Beijing Normal University, Beijing Language and Culture University and Nankai University. Registered with China’s Civil Affairs Ministry, the foundation is described by the Congressional Research Service as a nongovernmental charity sponsored by China’s Ministry of Education and composed of universities and corporations. In July 2020, the ministry renamed Hanban the Center for Language Education and Cooperation. The center retained Chinese proficiency testing, teaching materials and the “Chinese Bridge” program, while the foundation assumed funding and oversight of the remaining institutes and many replacement language programs. The global network then comprised 541 institutes and 1,170 Confucius Classrooms in 162 countries. Analysts quoted by China’s state-run Global Times said the restructuring would counter the Western view of the organization as China’s “ideological marketing machine.” At least 64 of the 104 colleges and universities that closed their institutes opened similar programs under new names or maintained close ties with former Chinese sponsors, the scholars’ association found . Institute employees moved into successor programs, and some textbooks remained on campus. A 2023 GAO survey found that 43 of 74 schools that closed an institute retained ties with their Chinese partner. Nine still received support, though eight schools said their partnerships predated the institutes. The College of William and Mary closed its Confucius Institute on June 30, 2021, then launched a partnership with the same Chinese partner, Beijing Normal University, the next day. The W&M-BNU Collaborative Partnership remains active, offering summer and winter study abroad, visiting student programs and cultural exchanges. In December 2021, Binghamton University established the Center for Theater Arts Collaboration with its former institute partner, the National Academy of Chinese Theatre Arts. The academy’s president, vice president, four department chairs and international exchange director serve on the center’s advisory board. An academy professor also teaches Beijing opera at Binghamton as a visiting professor. The University of Washington’s Confucius Institute, established under a 2009 Hanban agreement, moved to Pacific Lutheran University in Tacoma in 2020. It retained the Confucius name until its closure in summer 2026. Its Chinese partners were Sichuan University and Chongqing Jiaotong University, while Seattle Public Schools ran its K–12 education center. In 2022, Sichuan University reported that the institute served about 30 elementary and middle schools across eight districts. Western Kentucky University announced its institute’s closure on April 22, 2019. Within two months, the program moved to the Simpson County school district under a five-year agreement with Hanban and its existing Chinese partner, North China Electric Power University. Renamed the Confucius Institute of Western Kentucky, it served 47 K–12 schools across more than a dozen counties. BG Education Management Solutions, a nonprofit founded by former institute director Terrill Martin, operated it from July 2019 to June 2024. The National Academies excluded institutes hosted by school districts from its 2023 list of open institutes. At the program’s peak in 2017, China supported Confucius Classrooms in 501 American schools . The Foundation for Defense of Democracies’ October study found that BG Education Management Solutions maintained its partnership with North China Electric Power University. Other Chinese-funded exchanges have expanded. The Young Envoys Scholarship, launched in 2024 and run by the China Education Association for International Exchange, drew participants from about 83 universities and 27 K–12 schools, according to an August 2026 report by Defending Education, a parents’ advocacy group. In 2026, American Heritage Schools sent 31 students and faculty to China through the program, with the Chinese association covering most travel costs. The Pentagon’s funding restrictions apply only to host higher education institutions, leaving K–12 programs outside the ban. The post How Schools Hid Chinese Communist Party Ties After Hegseth Shut Down 80 Rebranded Confucius Institute Programs appeared first on The Gateway Pundit .

title: China’s Military Helicopters: A Guide
zh_title: 中国军用直升机：指南
summary: 中国人民解放军 (PLA) 拥有一支日益多样化的直升机机队，涵盖从基本飞行员训练和战场运输到空中预警、反潜战和专门攻击任务等各个领域。这支部队反映了数十年的发展，通常从从法国购买直升机开始，后来经许可生产，然后逐渐转向本土设计。结果是经过广泛现代化改造的旧飞机和围绕中国不断扩大的军事需求而设计的新平台的混合体，
content:
中国人民解放军 (PLA) 拥有一支日益多样化的直升机机队，涵盖从基本飞行员训练和战场运输到空中预警、反潜战和专门攻击任务等各个领域。这支部队反映了数十年的发展，通常从从法国购买直升机开始，后来经许可生产，然后逐渐转向本土设计。其结果是，经过大规模现代化改造的旧飞机和根据中国不断扩大的军事需求而设计的新平台，包括不断壮大的航母和两栖攻击舰队。 Z-10 攻击直升机。摄影：VCG/VCG via Getty Images Z-8 系列最初源自冷战时期的法国 Super Frelon，是这种演变的一个特别好的例子。它催生了各种专门的变体，包括搜索和救援、运输、电子战和机载指挥所直升机。与此同时，Z-20（经常被称为西科斯基 S-70/H-60 克隆版）已成为具有陆基、海军和攻击型的现代中型运输平台，而 Z-10 和更新的 Z-21 则代表了中国对专用攻击直升机的日益重视。 2024 年，中国南方广东省珠海市的珠海航展上，一架 Z-8C 飞机进行空中攻击演示。
CFOTO/Future Publishing via Getty Images 本指南探讨了解放军运营的主要直升机类型、它们的发展以及它们预期发挥的作用。同时，应该指出的是，就目前情况而言，解放军在各种应用中仍然严重依赖外国采购的直升机。俄罗斯制造的直升机为解放军提供了运输和特种海军能力的结合。 Mi-17/171 Hip 系列支持部队和货物运输、搜索和救援、特种作战以及选择高空或特定任务角色。在海上，Ka-28 Helix 提供反潜战能力，而 Ka-31 的雷达则支持机载舰队监视。这些飞机仍在服役，其既定能力继续满足作战需求。然而，它们越来越多地得到中国设计的补充，包括某些专门为提供直接替代品而定制的设计。解放军运营的最先进的直升机是用于战斗搜索和救援的 Mi-171Sh。它具有广泛的自我保护设备和武器。摄影：Sun Lin/VCG via Getty Images 实用、训练和轻型直升机 HC-120 HC-120 是一款轻型通用直升机，源自 EC120，EC120 是中国、法国和新加坡在 20 世纪 90 年代共同开发的设计。
该型号于 2005 年进入解放军陆军航空兵服役，为初级直升机训练提供了现代化平台，并取代了老化的 SA316 Alouette III。HC-120 由一台透博梅卡 Arrius 2F 涡轮轴发动机提供动力。它的推出代表了陆军航空训练机队现代化的重要一步，为飞行员在过渡到更大的作战类型之前提供了使用更现代的直升机的经验。一架 HC-120，采用陆军航空训练学校的颜色。来自中国互联网 Z-11 Z-11 是由昌河飞机工业公司（CHAIC）和 602 研究所开发的轻型通用直升机。该设计基于法国 AS350BA Écureuil ，其示例来自于

【原文 English Original】
China’s People’s Liberation Army (PLA) operates an increasingly diverse fleet of helicopters spanning everything from basic pilot training and battlefield transport to airborne early warning, anti-submarine warfare, and dedicated attack missions. The force reflects decades of development, often beginning with helicopters acquired from France and later produced under license, before transitioning to increasingly indigenous designs. The result is a mix of older aircraft that have undergone extensive modernization and newer platforms designed around the requirements of China’s expanding military, including its growing carrier and amphibious assault fleets . A Z-10 attack helicopter. Photo by VCG/VCG via Getty Images The Z-8 family, originally derived from the Cold War-era French Super Frelon , is a particularly good example of this evolution. It has spawned a wide range of specialized variants, including search and rescue, transport, electronic warfare, and airborne command post helicopters. Meanwhile, the Z-20 — frequently alluded to as a Sikorsky S-70/H-60 clone — has emerged as a modern medium-lift platform with land-based, naval, and assault variants, while the Z-10 and newer Z-21 represent China’s growing emphasis on dedicated attack helicopters. A PLAN Z-8C conducts an aerial assault demonstration at the Zhuhai Air Show in Zhuhai, south China’s Guangdong province, in 2024. CFOTO/Future Publishing via Getty Images This guide examines the principal helicopter types operated by the PLA, their development, and the roles they are expected to perform. At the same time, it should be noted that, as it now stands, the PLA remains heavily reliant on foreign-sourced helicopters for a wide variety of applications. Russian-built helicopters give the PLA a mix of transport and specialized naval capabilities. The Mi-17/171 Hip family supports troop and cargo movement, search and rescue, special operations, and select high-altitude or mission-specific roles. At sea, the Ka-28 Helix provides anti-submarine warfare, while the Ka-31’s radar supports airborne fleet surveillance. These aircraft remain in service where their established capabilities continue to meet operational needs. However, they are increasingly supplemented by Chinese designs, including certain designs that have been tailored to provide direct replacements. The most advanced Hip helicopter operated by the PLA is the Mi-171Sh used for combat search and rescue. It features extensive self-protection equipment and armament. Photo by Sun Lin/VCG via Getty Images Utility, Training, and Light Helicopters HC-120 The HC-120 is a light utility helicopter derived from the EC120, a design co-developed by China, France, and Singapore during the 1990s. The type entered service with PLA Army Aviation in 2005, providing a modern platform for primary helicopter training and replacing the aging SA316 Alouette III in that role. The HC-120 is powered by a single Turbomeca Arrius 2F turboshaft engine. Its introduction represented an important step in modernizing the Army Aviation training fleet, giving pilots experience with a more contemporary helicopter before transitioning to larger operational types. An HC-120 in the colors of the Army Aviation Training School. via Chinese internet Z-11 The Z-11 is a light utility helicopter developed by Changhe Aircraft Industries Corporation (CHAIC) and the 602 Research Institute. The design is based on the French AS350BA Écureuil , examples of which were acquired for Army Aviation. Deliveries of the Z-11 to Army Aviation began in 1998. The helicopter is powered by a single WZ-8D turboshaft engine and is primarily used for training, liaison, and other light utility duties. A scout and armed reconnaissance derivative, designated as the Z-11WB, was developed with a nose-mounted electro-optical (EO) turret and external weapon pylons capable of carrying rockets, missiles, and gun pods. Its operational status remains unclear, although it provided the basis for the unarmed Z-11A training helicopter used by the Army Aviation Academy. A demonstrator for the Z-11WB scout and armed reconnaissance helicopter. via Chinese internet The Z-8 Family: From French Origins To A Modern Helicopter Lineage Z-8J The Z-8 was developed from the French SA321Ja Super Frelon, 13 examples of which China purchased during the late 1970s. Changhe Aircraft Industries Corporation subsequently developed an indigenous version during the 1980s. Powered by three WZ-6 turboshaft engines, the original Z-8 became the foundation for a broad family of helicopters serving the PLA Navy (PLAN), Army Aviation, and People’s Liberation Army Air Force (PLAAF). The Z-8J is the naval transport variant, with a boat-like hull. For anti-submarine warfare (ASW) missions, the helicopter can be equipped with a surface-search radar, a French HS-12 dipping sonar, and Whitehead A244S or ET52 torpedoes. Several specialized derivatives were developed from the Z-8J: Z-8S: A naval search and rescue (SAR) version with upgraded avionics, a searchlight, a forward-looking infrared (FLIR) turret, and a rescue hoist. Most Z-8Js have reportedly been upgraded to this configuration. Z-8JH: A medical evacuation and SAR variant. The Z-8J and Z-8JH have both been used aboard Chinese aircraft carriers, providing transport and support capabilities for embarked naval forces. A Z-8JH on the PLAN replenishment ship Kekexilihu at Qingdao Port, Shandong Province of China, in 2023. Photo by Fu Tian/China News Service/VCG via Getty Images Z-8C The Z-8C represents a substantially improved successor to the original naval Z-8J series. The helicopter was first reported in 2016 and incorporates a number of changes intended to improve its performance and operational versatility. The most visible differences include a redesigned nose with a chin-mounted weather radar, a FLIR turret, and a pilot night-vision system (PNVS) mounted above the cockpit. A searchlight is also fitted, while the longer engine compartment accommodates the WZ-6C turboshaft engine. The Z-8C is operated by the PLA Marine Corps, while the Z-8CJ serves as a training variant with the Naval Aviation University. The helicopter has become a principal transport platform for the Type 075 amphibious assault ship, supporting the movement of troops and equipment between ships and shore. Z-8C helicopters conduct aerial display training for the upcoming Airshow China in Zhuhai, Guangdong Province of China, in 2024. Photo by Chen Xiao/VCG via Getty Images Z-8K/KA The PLAAF introduced the Z-8K in 2007 as a dedicated search-and-rescue helicopter. The related Z-8KA is configured for combat search and rescue (CSAR), including the recovery of personnel from hostile or contested environments. Both versions feature a FLIR turret, searchlight, radar-warning receiver (RWR), chaff and flare dispensers, and a rescue hoist. Some aircraft are also equipped with small terrain-following radars beneath the nose to support low-level operations. Selected helicopters have received satellite communications (SATCOM) antennas on top of the tail boom, improving their communications capabilities over longer distances. A further derivative, the Z-8KH, was developed for the PLAAF garrison stationed in Hong Kong. This version is distinguished by chaff and flare dispensers integrated into its flotation equipment. A Z-8KA helicopter during the 2022 Changchun Air Show at Changchun Dafangshen Airport, Jilin Province of China. Photo by VCG/VCG via Getty Images Z-8B The Z-8B entered service with PLA Army Aviation in 2011 as an improved transport helicopter. It shares several characteristics with the Z-8KH but lacks the latter’s flotation equipment. The Z-8B incorporates a glass cockpit and has become a major component of the Army Aviation transport fleet. Some aircraft have subsequently had flotation equipment reinstalled, reflecting the type’s continuing evolution. An optional auxiliary fuel tank can be installed inside the cabin to extend its range. Other upgrades have included SATCOM antennas on the tail boom and, on some aircraft, WZ-6C engines, an EO turret, and a terrain-following radar beneath the nose. A specialized operations variant has also been identified. These helicopters incorporate RWR, laser-warning receivers (LWR), and missile-approach warning system (MAWS) sensors, alongside flare dispensers and ceramic armor protection. A still from a CCTV video shows a Z-8B equipped with RWR, LWR, and MAWS sensors, as well as countermeasures dispensers. via Chinese internet Z-8G Lacking the boat-like hull of the Z-8B, the Z-8G is expected to replace that type in Army Aviation service. The helicopter was evaluated from 2014 and was specifically optimized for operations at high altitudes, including in Tibet. Unlike earlier Z-8 variants, the initial Z-8G configuration uses imported Pratt & Whitney Canada PT6B-67A turboshaft engines. Its redesigned nose is longer and more aerodynamically efficient, while the glass cockpit and terrain-following radar support operations in demanding environments. The helicopter also incorporates SATCOM and BeiDou/GPS antennas to improve communications and navigation during long-range missions. Some Z-8Gs have been equipped for special operations, with combinations of MAWS, RWR, and LWR sensors mounted on the rear fuselage and sponsons, together with chaff and flare dispensers. Armor plates beneath the cockpit windows provide additional protection, and some aircraft carry a 12.7mm machine gun inside a cabin doorway. Several specialized variants have also been identified: A battlefield electronic-warfare helicopter featuring large cylindrical antennas mounted on both sides of the mid-fuselage. Another electronic warfare configuration reportedly uses rectangular plate antenna arrays mounted on both sides of the rear fuselage. An airborne command-post variant featuring a retractable synthetic-aperture radar (SAR) surveillance system inside the rear fuselage, alongside additional electronic-support-measures (ESM) antennas. Some Z-8Gs may also have adopted the indigenous WZ-6C engine. A Z-8G at Airshow China at Zhuhai in 2024. Photo by Costfoto/NurPhoto via Getty Images Z-8L The Z-8L is a wide-body development of the Z-8G that first flew in 2017. Its most prominent feature is a pair of large sponsons mounted along the sides of the fuselage, providing additional space for fuel tanks and other equipment. The wider fuselage also increases internal volume, allowing the helicopter to carry more cargo and equipment. Relocating the internal fuel tanks beneath the cabin floor has further increased usable cabin space. Some aircraft have been observed with RWR and MAWS sensors on both sides of the forward fuselage, a roof-mounted FLIR turret, and a terrain-following radar beneath the nose. Additional defensive equipment, including LWR and RWR sensors and chaff/flare dispensers, can be installed on the sponsons. A SATCOM antenna is mounted on top of the tail boom. The original PT6B-67A engines are reportedly being replaced by the more powerful indigenous WZ-7 turboshaft. The Z-8L provides the Army with a larger and more capable transport helicopter suited to demanding operating environments and specialized missions. A Z-8L (nearest camera) alongside a Z-20 during the 2022 Airshow China in Zhuhai, Guangdong province of China. Photo by Stringer/Anadolu Agency via Getty Images Z-8D The Z-8D is a shipborne derivative of the Z-8L that first appeared in 2023. It combines the wide-body configuration with an extensive self-defense suite intended to improve survivability during operations over water. The helicopter features RWR, LWR, and MAWS sensors, along with chaff and flare dispensers. Four inflatable flotation units provide emergency protection in the event of a forced landing at sea. Power is supplied by either WZ-6C or the newer WZ-7 turboshaft engines. Engine air particle separators (EAPS) are installed ahead of the engine inlets to reduce the risk of damage from airborne debris. The Z-8D is expected to operate from China’s Type 075 amphibious assault ships and the larger Type 076 amphibious assault ship. One of the first clear images of a PLAN Naval Aviation Z-8D. via Chinese internet The Z-18 Series: Naval Utility, Early Warning, and ASW Helicopters Z-18Y Named White Heron, the Z-18Y was developed by the 602 Research Institute and Changhe as a new medium-lift shipborne transport helicopter. It is derived from the AC313 but incorporates a redesigned fuselage and a number of changes intended to improve its naval suitability. The helicopter uses imported PT6B-67A turboshaft engines and provides greater internal volume and payload capacity than the earlier Z-8. Improved performance in hot-and-high conditions is another important feature. The Z-18Y incorporates a nose-mounted weather radar and an FLIR/TV turret, along with additional communication and navigation antennas beneath the fuselage. A SATCOM antenna is installed on top of the tail boom. Folding main and tail rotor blades allow the helicopter to be stored more efficiently aboard ships. The Z-18Y is primarily used for carrier onboard delivery (COD) missions, transporting personnel and supplies between ships and shore. It has also provided the basis for several specialized naval derivatives. A Z-18Y operating from a Type 075 class assault ship. PLA Z-18J Named Bat, the Z-18J is an airborne early warning and control (AEW&C) helicopter developed from the Z-18Y. Its principal feature is a retractable radar antenna housed within a redesigned rear fuselage. The long-range, multimode AESA radar is lowered vertically during operation, providing 360-degree coverage around the helicopter. The Z-18J also incorporates a nose-mounted FLIR turret and additional MAWS and RWR antennas distributed around the nose and rear fuselage. Chaff and flare dispensers are installed in the flotation equipment. The helicopter has been used aboard Chinese aircraft carriers as an interim airborne early-warning platform and has also been observed operating from Type 075 amphibious assault ships. A rescue hoist is installed on the starboard side of the forward fuselage, allowing the aircraft to perform secondary SAR duties. An improved Z-18A features a redesigned engine and gearbox compartment and three indigenous WZ-6C engines. Some Z-18Js and Z-18As have also received SATCOM antennas to improve long-range communications. A Z-18J together with two J-15 fighters onboard the Liaoning . via Chinese internet Z-18F Named Sea Eagle, the Z-18F is an ASW and anti-ship warfare helicopter developed from the Z-18Y. It first appeared in 2014 and represents a substantial improvement over the earlier Z-8-based naval ASW helicopters. The helicopter incorporates a large surface-search radar beneath the nose, while its FLIR/TV turret has been relocated to the starboard side of the fuselage. A dipping sonar provides an additional means of detecting submarines, while MAWS and RWR antennas are installed on the forward and rear fuselage. Additional communications and navigation antennas are mounted beneath the fuselage. Four external pylons can carry torpedoes or anti-ship missiles (AShMs), including the YJ-9. A dispenser near the rear loading ramp allows the helicopter to deploy sonobuoys. The Z-18F operates aboard Chinese aircraft carriers and the Type 075 amphibious assault ship. Several improved derivatives have since appeared: Z-18FA: Incorporates a redesigned engine and gearbox compartment and three domestic WZ-6C turboshaft engines. Z-18FG: Features a new chin-mounted search radar and small side pylons for lightweight ASW torpedoes or AShMs. Z-18FB: A further improved version reportedly powered by three WZ-7 turboshaft engines, replacing the Canadian PT6B-67A. These developments point to a continuing effort to improve the Z-18’s performance and extend the operational life of the broader family. A Z-18F assigned to the aircraft carrier Liaoning . via Chinese internet The Z-9 Family Z-9A/B The Z-9 originated from the French AS365 Dauphin family, with China acquiring aircraft and subsequently producing them under license through Harbin Aircraft Industry Group (HAIG) during the 1990s. The Z-9A became a principal utility helicopter for Army Aviation and was also used for pilot training. The improved Z-9B incorporated a greater proportion of indigenous components, helping establish the foundation for China’s broader Z-9 development program, which also took it in a maritime direction. The helicopter has since become one of China’s most widely used light utility platforms and has also been widely exported in the Z-9E series. Cambodian soldiers stand in front of Z-9s during a handover ceremony at a Royal Cambodian Air Force base in Phnom Penh, in 2013. KHEM SOVANNARA/AFP via Getty Images KHEM SOVANNARA Z-9C The Z-9C is China’s indigenous naval derivative of the French AS565 Panther , examples of which were imported during the late 1980s. The helicopter incorporates a domestically developed surface-search radar and dipping sonar, allowing it to conduct ASW missions. It can carry up to two Yu-7K torpedoes and is equipped with inflatable flotation bags for emergency landings on water. Some Z-9Cs have been converted to SAR duties, receiving a searchlight, an EO turret, and a rescue hoist. The type has also been used for anti-piracy patrols off the Somali coast. In this role, some aircraft have carried a 12.7mm gun pod and a 57mm rocket launcher. A downgraded training version was developed for the Naval Aviation Academy. Z-9 sits aboard the Type 052D destroyer Zhanjiang at Ngong Shuen Chau Naval Base on Stonecutters Island in Hong Kong on July 6, 2025. Photo by AFP Z-9D The Z-9D is an improved derivative of the Z-9C, incorporating a greater emphasis on anti-surface warfare. The helicopter features stub wings capable of carrying up to four AShMs for use against smaller surface targets. A new fire-control radar is housed in a larger nose cone, while the weapon-control officer is positioned in the rear cabin. RWR antennas are installed on both sides of the nose and near the tail rotor. The Z-9D has been observed operating from Type 056 and Type 056A frigates. Some aircraft have also received an EO turret beneath the fuselage, expanding their surveillance and targeting capabilities. A Z-9D carrying a YJ-9 anti-ship missile. via Chinese internet Z-9F The Z-9F is an improved ASW helicopter based on the Z-9D. It was first observed in 2017 and is expected to replace the older Z-9C. The helicopter incorporates a new dipping sonar, a glass cockpit, and an improved surface-search radar. A BeiDou antenna is mounted on top of the cabin. The Z-9F retains the ability to carry up to two ASW torpedoes beneath its stub wings, providing a more modern platform for shipborne submarine-hunting missions. Z-9S The Z-9S is a naval search-and-rescue helicopter developed for operations aboard Chinese aircraft carriers. It features a nose-mounted EO turret, a searchlight, and a rescue hoist installed on the starboard side. The helicopter is also used for training by the Naval Aviation University. A small number of SAR-configured Z-9S helicopters are also operated by Army Aviation. A Z-9S conducts exercises onboard a Type 055 destroyer. via Chinese internet Z-9WA/WZ The Z-9WA is a night-attack development of the Z-9W, incorporating more powerful engines and improved avionics for operations in low-light conditions. The helicopter features stub wings capable of carrying up to eight KD-8 anti-tank guided missiles (ATGMs) or PL-90 air-to-air missiles (AAMs). A nose-mounted low-light TV/IR turret supports night operations, while RWR antennas are installed on both sides of the fuselage. Additional features include cockpit armor, flare dispensers, a datalink, and a redesigned cockpit compatible with night-vision goggles (NVGs). Z-9WZ. via Chinese internet The improved Z-9WZ incorporates a laser designator, allowing it to employ the newer KD-9 ATGM, as well as FN-6 AAMs. It is also powered by WZ-8H engines. Most Z-9WAs are believed to have been upgraded to the WZ standard. The PLAAF operates some Z-9WA/WZ helicopters in the SAR role. A similar derivative, the Z-9ZH, is used by the PLAAF garrison stationed in Hong Kong. Dedicated Attack and Scout Helicopters Z-10 The Z-10 represents China’s first dedicated modern attack helicopter. Developed by the 602 Research Institute, CHAIC, and HAIG, the program also received early input from Russia’s Kamov design bureau. The helicopter features a conventional tandem-seat gunship configuration, with the gunner seated in front and the pilot behind. A five-blade composite main rotor and distinctive scissor-type tail rotor distinguish the design. The Z-10 is powered by WZ-9 turboshaft engines and entered service in 2010, following its first flight in 2003. A Z-10K at the Shek Kong Barracks in Hong Kong, China. Photo by Zhang Xiangyi/China News Service/VCG via Getty Images Its primary armament consists of up to eight KD-9 or KD-10 laser-guided ATGMs, supplemented by a chin-mounted 23mm chain gun. The helicopter can also carry up to eight PL-90 AAMs. The nose-mounted PNVS and target acquisition and designation system (TADS)-equivalent housing incorporates FLIR, a TV camera, a laser rangefinder, and a laser designator. RWR antennas are installed on both sides of the forward and aft fuselage, while LWR sensors are mounted on the pylon tips. The initial prototypes were powered by the Pratt & Whitney Canada PT6C-76C engine. Series-production aircraft instead adopted the less powerful WZ-9, resulting in reductions to armor protection, sensor size, and weapon load compared with the original configuration. Several variants and upgrades have since emerged: Z-10H: Retains the original PNVS/TADS configuration while using WZ-9 engines. Z-10K: A dedicated version for PLAAF airborne units, featuring a new 23mm gun and 19-tube rocket launchers. Some aircraft have SATCOM antennas on top of the tail boom. Z-10A: The definitive production configuration, distinguished by upward-facing engine exhaust nozzles. Later upgrades: Some Z-10 and Z-10K aircraft have received additional ceramic armor, MAWS sensors on the nose, and SATCOM antennas for long-range communications. The helicopter has also gained newer long-range, IIR/CCD-guided ATGMs. These weapons require an additional datalink antenna mounted in front of the PNVS. Later developments include the introduction of millimeter-wave (MMW) radar-guided fire-and-forget missiles, potentially allowing the Z-10 to operate alongside the Z-19 in coordinated attack missions. The export-oriented Z-10ME incorporates further improvements, including a mast-mounted MMW radar. Z-19 The Z-19 is a scout and attack helicopter developed by HAIG using the H425 as its basis. It was intended to replace the Z-9WA while complementing the larger Z-10. The helicopter features a narrow fuselage and tandem cockpit, with the pilot seated in front and the gunner behind. A nose-mounted EO turret incorporates FLIR, a TV camera, and a laser rangefinder, while RWR antennas provide warning of hostile radar emissions. The Z-19 uses the same WZ-8C engines, transmission, and rotor systems as the H425, helping accelerate its development. A Z-19 without the mast-mounted MMW radar. via Chinese internet When fitted with a mast-mounted MMW radar, the Z-19 provides additional target-detection capabilities. The helicopter’s armament is broadly similar to that of the Z-9WA, including KD-9 and KD-10 ATGMs, PL-90 AAMs, rocket launchers, and gun pods. Later upgrades include MAWS sensors on the nose and tail, along with LWR sensors on the stub wings. The Z-19 has also been integrated with newer long-range IIR/CCD/laser-guided ATGMs, including the KF-9, KF-10, and KF-11. These weapons require an additional datalink antenna mounted on the nose. Z-21 The Z-21 is a new heavy attack helicopter first identified in 2024. Developed by the 602 Research Institute, Changhe, and Hafei, it appears to be a substantially larger and more heavily protected gunship than the Z-10. The helicopter is believed to use the WZ-10 turboshaft engines and rotor systems developed for the Z-20. It features a conventional tandem-seat configuration, with a gunner in the front and a pilot behind. One of the first photos of the Z-21. via Chinese internet Large cheek fairings on either side of the fuselage incorporate MAWS, LWR, ESM, and electronic countermeasures (ECM) equipment. The nose features a new PNVS above a TADS, while an MMW search radar is mounted above the main rotor mast. Laser-powered directional infrared countermeasures (DIRCM) are installed on the wingtips. Additional defensive equipment includes chaff and flare dispensers on the cheek fairings and tail boom. A BeiDou antenna is mounted on the tail boom, while at least one prototype has been observed with upward-facing engine exhausts. Z-21. via Chinese internet The Z-21 is expected to feature a 30mm chain gun beneath the forward fuselage. Each stub wing incorporates three weapon stations capable of carrying the newer KF-series long-range ATGMs, PL-90 AAMs, and other emerging weapons. Compared with the Z-20, the Z-21 is expected to offer improved high-altitude performance, greater armor protection, and a heavier payload, making it better suited to demanding attack missions. The Z-20 Family: China’s New Medium Helicopter Z-20 The Z-20 is China’s new medium-lift general-purpose helicopter, developed by the 602 Research Institute, Harbin, and Changhe since the late 1990s. The design is heavily influenced by the Sikorsky S-70 Black Hawk , examples of which China acquired for the PLA during the 1980s. However, the Z-20 incorporates a number of indigenous systems and is intended to replace the Mi-17 series in Army Aviation service. The helicopter features a five-blade main rotor, a glass cockpit, and armor protection around the cockpit. A PNVS is mounted beneath the chin, while RWR antennas are installed on both sides of the forward and rear fuselage. Additional equipment includes LWR sensors on both sides of the nose, SATCOM, ECM antennas on top of the fuselage, and a nose-mounted weather radar and terrain-following radar. A Z-20 during the 7th China Helicopter Exposition in Tianjin Municipality, China, in 2025. Photo by VCG/VCG via Getty Images The Z-20 is powered by two WZ-10 turboshaft engines and can carry up to 13 fully equipped soldiers. An optional fuel tank can be installed in the cargo compartment to extend its range. Stub wings can be fitted to carry rocket launchers, gun pods, and external fuel tanks. The Z-20 first flew in 2013 and entered service with PLA Army Aviation by 2019. Several aircraft have been observed with upward-facing engine exhausts. A SAR variant incorporates an EO turret and searchlight beneath the forward fuselage, together with a rescue hoist above the cabin door. Z-20K/KS/KT The Z-20 has also spawned a number of specialized variants for the PLAAF. The Z-20K, identified in 2022, is a transport helicopter intended for airborne assault units. The PLAAF operates the Z-20KS subvariant in the SAR role. This model features an EO turret and searchlight beneath the forward fuselage, while optional stub wings allow it to carry rocket launchers and gun pods. An improved assault variant, the Z-20KT, incorporates a larger SATCOM antenna on top of the tail boom. Its folding tail section indicates that the helicopter is designed to facilitate aerial transport, allowing rapid deployment over long distances. A Z-20K at the Shek Kong Barracks in Hong Kong, China, in 2026. Photo by VCG/VCG via Getty Images Z-20T The Z-20T is a specialized assault helicopter broadly comparable in concept to the MH-60L Direct Action Penetrator used by the U.S. Army. The helicopter features large stub wings capable of carrying KD-9 and KD-10 ATGMs, KF-9A ATGMs, PL-90 AAMs, ECM pods, and external fuel tanks. LWR sensors have been relocated to the wingtips, while a TADS has replaced the weather radar in the nose. Additional armor plates provide increased protection for the crew and critical systems. Later examples have also been observed with upward-facing engine exhausts. Air Cavalry: Footage shows Z-20T assault helicopters effectively boosting the tactical flexibility of the Chinese PLA Army’s heliborne troops during an air assault training exercise. #Helicopter #AirAssault #Z20T #Z10 #PLA #Army #ChinaMilitary #ChinaMilBugle pic.twitter.com/NcoMbsz9gP — China Military Bugle (@ChinaMilBugle) May 1, 2026 Z-20F The Z-20F is a shipborne ASW helicopter developed to provide the PLAN with a modern equivalent to the MH-60R Seahawk . It first flew in 2018. The helicopter incorporates folding rotor blades and a folding tail boom to facilitate shipboard storage. An emergency flotation system is fitted, while the rear landing gear has been relocated forward to the rear end of the fuselage. The redesigned nose features an EO/laser-ranging turret, with a surface-search radar antenna mounted beneath the chin. A SATCOM antenna is installed on top of the tail boom. Additional ESM antennas are distributed around the nose and rear fuselage. A 25-round sonobuoy launcher is mounted on the port side, while a dipping sonar and rescue hoist provide additional ASW and SAR capabilities. The Z-20F can carry up to four YJ-9 AShMs beneath its stub wings, alongside lightweight ASW torpedoes on rear fuselage pylons. The helicopter is expected to replace the older Z-9C on Type 054 frigates and Type 052 and Type 055 destroyers. It has also been observed aboard the aircraft carrier Fujian and Type 075 amphibious assault ships. A Z-20F on the deck of the carrier Fujian carrying a pair of YJ-9 anti-ship missiles under one stub wing. via Chinese internet Z-20J The Z-20J is a shipborne transport and assault variant designed for the PLAN. Its stub wings can carry up to eight KD-9 ATGMs or four YJ-9 AShMs, as well as rocket launchers, external fuel tanks, and gun pods. MAWS sensors are installed on both sides of the chin and along the rear fuselage, providing additional protection during operations over water. The Z-20J expands the range of missions that can be performed from Chinese surface combatants and amphibious assault ships, complementing the ASW-focused Z-20F. Z-20J. via Chinese internet Conclusion Despite often being overshadowed by the PLA’s latest combat aircraft , missiles , and other high-profile weapons programs, helicopters remain an indispensable part of China’s military modernization. They provide critical capabilities, from moving troops and supplies across difficult terrain to supporting amphibious operations, special forces, search and rescue, and naval warfare. More importantly, the steady development of indigenous helicopter designs reflects China’s determination to reduce reliance on foreign suppliers and build a more capable, self-sufficient rotary-wing force. These aircraft may attract less attention than the PLA’s newest fighters, but their growing sophistication and expanding roles make them an essential part of the force’s ability to operate across a wide range of contingencies. Contact the author: thomas@thewarzone.com The post China’s Military Helicopters: A Guide appeared first on TWZ .

content:
圖為美國芯片公司英偉達的一款芯片。(JOEL SAGET/AFP via Getty Images)
【大紀元2026年11月06日訊】（大紀元記者林燕綜合報導）週四（11月5日），路透社引述知情人士的消息稱，約60萬枚英偉達（Nvidia）先進芯片滯留香港，等待北京批准後進入中國大陸。這凸顯了中國科技公司對頂尖芯片的需求，以及中共當局繼續用審批推遲來卡中企的脖子。
報導指，這批H200芯片的庫存規模消息是首次披露，反映出北京不願意加深對美國先進技術的依賴。
換句話說，中共對先進芯片進口的「卡脖子」做法，成為這批英偉達芯片進入中國的主要障礙。
三位知情人士表示，北京近幾個月來已允許部分芯片入境，但被批准放行是很少一部分，當局尚未批准向中國大陸大量進口此類產品。其中一位知情人士稱，幾家中國大型互聯網公司在過去幾個月裡各自獲得了約1萬顆H200芯片。
三位知情人士表示，少量芯片已通過中間商和間接渠道運抵中國，但未透露具體數量。
H200並非英偉達最新的AI處理器，但它擁有中國同類產品目前尚無法匹敵的功能，使其在訓練AI模型方面非常有用，尤其是在與英偉達軟件結合使用時。
英偉達芯片滯留香港凸顯了中共當局的矛盾，一方面希望獲得西方芯片的先進計算能力。另一方面，又不希望過度依賴美國芯片。
今年5月，英偉達首席執行官黃仁勛表示，英偉達已經獲得美國政府許可，可以向中國銷售H200芯片，但仍未獲得北京批准。
人工智能政策與戰略研究院（IAPS）研究員徐森凱（Karson Elmgren）在X上發文表示，中方行為確實讓人難以理解。他說，這些尖端芯片是如今這個科技工業革命時代最重要的，「中方為啥不願意進口這些原材料，有點難理解」。
彼得森國際經濟研究所（Peterson Institute for International Economics）高級研究員馬永哲（Martin Chorzempa）也回帖說，中方可能是認為，扶持國內芯片設計商與製造商所帶來的收益，大於短期提升AI能力的收益。
路透社還提到，因供應受限，一些中國買家通過中介和間接渠道購買H200芯片，進一步推高了黑市價格。一位知情人士表示，截至10月底，一台八卡H200服務器在中國的報價超過600萬元人民幣（約90萬美元），大約是一年前價格的三倍。這名人士還表示，採用英偉達更新的Blackwell芯片且受美國出口管制的服務器，單台報價更超過2000萬元人民幣。
科技媒體The Information 7月份報導，中方官員已告知包括阿里巴巴、字節跳動和DeepSeek在內的多家公司，它們可以獲准購買數量有限的H200芯片用於訓練人工智能模型。
但報導稱，獲批芯片總數可能不足20萬枚，因為北京仍希望這些公司優先使用國產處理器進行推理。

content: 作者：刘瑜 原载《南方周末》旗下“弎聲” 20220722 当秦晖先生试图给“文化的冲突”指出“制度的出路”时，对其难度，当然不可能没有认识。但是，“怀绝望之心，行希望之事”，是其知识分子深沉的天真。 秦晖先生很像是一个思想的管道工。哪里出现了认识和观念的严重堵塞，他就常常“赶赴现场”，进行疏通清理。虽然专业背景是中国古代史，但他传奇般的知识面、记忆力和思辨力使其“管道疏通”工作远远超出了中国古代史领域。从中国土地史到南非的城市化，从前苏东地区的私有化到中国当代的转型机制，秦晖先生总是能三下五除二，一方面拨乱反正，另一方面又警惕矫枉过正，将一堆杂乱无序的论争梳理得一清二楚。 他的作品是其将知识梳理能力运用到清末民初史的一次尝试。表面而言，是一个大杂烩式的文集，综合了秦先生对清末到1949年这一历史时期的分析与评价。仔细阅读，会发现“大杂烩”背后，有清晰的逻辑与层层递进的追问。 成功还是失败 追问的第一层，是辛亥革命到底成功了还是失败了？更确切地说，作为辛亥革命的成果——中华民国——在大陆时期的表现，到底有没有、有多少“成就”可言？ 以往的看法是，由于资产阶级的软弱性，革命没有能发动群众，尤其是农民，导致革命成果被军阀们攫取，造成连年的军阀混战。这个逻辑是如此深入人心，以至于今天中国人看到“军阀混战”四个字，不用交代时间地点，往往会本能地联想到“北洋时期”。 对此，秦晖老师花了大量篇幅进行追问，并从经济、外交甚至政治几个角度做出分析。就经济而言，秦晖先生通过横向的国际比较以及纵向的历史比较，试图说明大陆时期的民国其实取得了相当的经济成就。一个突出的表现，就是中国人口史上罕见的“乱世增长”——在中国历史上，“改朝换代”的乱世往往伴随着人口剧减，幅度常常高达人口规模的一半左右，但是民国时期，除了抗战阶段，人口实现了前所未有的“乱世增长”。 更详细的论证，是在外交领域。尽管民国时期的中国始终被外敌——尤其是日、俄两国——虎视眈眈，尽管辛亥革命时期的中国背负着各种沉重的“不平等条约”，但是，民国的各种军事和外交努力使得中国从义和团时期列强眼中的排外“怪兽”变成了二战结束后的联合国安理会常任理事国之一。两次世界大战中的“正确站队”，华盛顿会议开启的“废约修约”行动，收回关税自主权，废除领事裁判权等等，使得中国作为一个所谓“半殖民地社会”部分“站起来了”。如果说还有没“站起来”的地方，应该说是苏俄通过雅尔塔体系给中国主权投下的长长阴影，从东北到蒙古，再到新疆，这道阴影到中华人民共和国时期才慢慢消退——其中一些则成了永久的伤疤。 即使是政治上，似乎也不能一概而论辛亥革命和民国时期失败了。清末民初的各种乱象，在秦晖先生看来，是中国历史上“治乱循环”中的一个周期。民初的军阀割据与混战，某种意义上来看，和东汉末年、晚唐、北朝后期军阀混战的机制类似，与其说都是“军阀”的罪过，不如说是积重难返的王朝巨轮转身时掀起的风浪。事实上，相比历史上人口动辄减半的周期性灾难，民初的这一次转身的“水花”已经压得很低了。 1945年6月，在旧金山召开了联合国国际组织会议，中华民国派出了以国民政府行政院代理院长宋子文为首的代表团，参加了这次会议，并签署了《联合国宪章》。图为代表团成员、驻英大使顾维钧在会议上发言。 启蒙为何失败 这就引出了的第二层追问：清末民初的启蒙为什么失败？ 在分析“什么原因”之前，秦晖先生花费了相当笔墨分析“不是什么原因”。一种常见的观点，也是保守主义者常常持有的观点，就是“革命过于激进论”。根据这种观点，如果清末民初中国人选择了“改良”而不是“革命”，采取了君主立宪而非共和革命，也许后面的悲剧能够得以避免。对这种观点，秦晖先生表达了不同意见。历史上的“君主立宪”大多发生在“封建主义”的历史传统中（比如西北欧各国），而官僚集权型专制（比如俄罗斯、奥斯曼、中国）往往只有依靠革命才能挣脱其深厚的专制体制。也就是说，不是“革命过于激进”导致了转型失败，而是转型僵局导致了“激进革命”。更何况，如果以变革是否暴力来区分激进与否，那么革命未必激进，而改良未必温和——辛亥革命本身流血并不多，而确立“君主立宪”的日本明治维新则伴随着相当规模的暴力战争。 另一种常见的看法，是李泽厚先生提出的“救亡压倒启蒙”。这是对启蒙失败的民族主义解释。根据这个观点，由于帝国主义的威胁，尤其是日本的入侵，导致民族主义情绪高涨，从而压倒了新文化时期的启蒙精神。秦晖先生同样质疑了这种看法。在他看来，不是“救亡”压倒了“启蒙”，而是“一种启蒙”压倒了“另一种启蒙”，确切地说，“日式启蒙”（国家主义）压倒了“西式启蒙”（民主主义）。时间上来说，也不是抗日时期的民族主义压倒了新文化时期的启蒙，而是新文化时期的“日式启蒙”压倒了清末的“西式启蒙”。也就是说，民族主义的高涨与其说是自由主义衰败的原因，不如说是其后果。 什么叫“日式启蒙”，什么叫“西式启蒙”？用秦晖先生的语言体系来说，“日式启蒙”就是个人打破小共同体（家庭、社区、社团、亲缘关系等等）的束缚，但是投入到“国家主义”的大共同体怀抱当中——这种“六亲不认”的个人主义表面上是一种个性解放，实际上成为国家主义甚至军国主义的共谋。而“西式启蒙”，则是一种以大共同体（国家、政府、皇帝）为主要抗争对象的个人主义——只有在这个基础上，才生长出真正的宪制精神以及宪制主义赖以生存的民间组织资源。秦晖说，清末民初，由于大量知识分子留学日本，他们深受“日式个人主义”的影响，追求个性解放、冲破“礼教束缚”，积极反对小共同体意识强烈的“儒家”，却在“富国强兵”的旗帜下投奔了国家主义。也就是说，知识分子从清末的“反法”到民初的“反儒”，构成了历史的倒退。 以小共同体精神的萎缩、大共同体精神的张扬来解释中国启蒙的失败，秦晖先生这方面的分析力透纸背，可以说道出了启蒙凋零的核心机制。不过，这种危险倾向的来源是日本还是“本地土特产”，则可以争议。毕竟，中国自身这种“扬大共同体、抑小共同体”的传统“源远流长”，从商鞅、韩非时代就已经登峰造极，恐怕无需“引进外资”。儒家思想（秦晖笔下的“古儒”）被法家狙击或吸纳，也不是从新文化时期开始，而是中国历史的一条若隐若现的主线。因此，民国初年此类思潮的兴起，与其说是吸收了错误的外来思想资源，不如说是没能克服自己的历史遗产。说到底，知识群体对外来思潮的选择性吸收，国家主义启蒙压倒了民主启蒙，并非偶然发生，恰恰因为外来的“国家主义”与传统中“欲为其国，必伐其聚”的“国家主义”一拍即合，才能够实现成功对接。 逃离历史的“诅咒” 在这个问题上，或许可以这样总结秦晖先生的观点：从文化回到制度。面对“数千年未有之变局”，清末民初这100年左右，知识分子们把太多精力花费在“中西文化之辩”上了，对此，秦晖先生曾经精辟地总结：文化无高下，制度有优劣。你爱打篮球我爱打乒乓球，游戏本身并无高下之分，不能说乒乓球还是篮球更“优越”，但是游戏规则却有优劣——如果一个游戏规则只让一方有发球权、让裁判同时担任运动员、让一方六个人上场另一方三个人上场，不管用在篮球还是乒乓球上，显然这是一个劣等的游戏规则。 作品中，有很大一部分在辨析太平天国和义和团的历史。显然，太平天国引入“中国特色的基督教”，而义和团狂热地排外反基督教，两者似乎构成文化的两极。然而，看似两极化的文化选择，其实共生在“秦制”的制度框架中。太平天国在基督教的外衣下，藏着法家“焚书坑儒”的灵魂，而义和团似乎披着捍卫本土文化的外衣，却难逃“跪着造反”的跪姿。也就是说，任何文化，如果不能摆脱传统的专制框架，都不大可能有自由生长、各美其美的空间。即使是所谓“古儒” “真儒”，也只有摆脱了“法儒”“伪儒”，才可能恢复其被抑制的优雅与舒展。 因此，转型之难不在于如何在“中西文化”之间做出一个选择，而在于如何构建一个尊重“底线自由”的制度来呵护多元文化的生长。不过，当秦晖先生小心翼翼地将“文化”与“制度”剥离时，似乎策略性地忽视了这一事实：对很多人来说，文化的核心就是关于制度的理念。也就是说，对相当一部分人，文化的要旨并不是爱吃饺子还是三明治，爱穿旗袍还是西装，爱打篮球还是爱打乒乓球，而是到底要建构一个以“秦制”还是“周制”、“西式个人主义”还是“日式个人主义” 为基础的制度。显然，如果文化包括关于公共生活如何组织的政治理念，而不仅仅是关于个人偏好的生活理念，那么，“制度有高下”必然推导出“文化有高下” ——那种尊重“底线自由”的政治文化观念“高于”那种蔑视这一“底线自由”的文化观念，那种认为裁判不能同时是运动员的文化观念“高于”那种认为裁判可以同时是运动员的文化观念。指出这一点之所以重要，是因为，知识分子追求“共同的底线”固然很重要，但是从政治上而言，“秦制”爱好者和“周制”爱好者之间并不存在共同的底线。对此保持清醒认识，有助于我们认识政治冲突中理性的边界，更重要的是，认识到所谓“制度底线”的前提是一定的“文化共识”（至少是“政治文化共识”）。 建设这种“政治文化的共识”，或许正是知识分子所能着力之处。一方面，清醒地意识到理性的边界——不是所有的政治 问题都能“政治地”解决，另一方面，仍然倾尽全力去构筑公共理性。当秦晖先生试图给“文化的冲突”指出“制度的出路”时，对其难度，当然不可能没有认识。但是，“怀绝望之心，行希望之事”，是其知识分子深沉的天真。韦伯曾说：政治是对硬木强劲而缓慢的击打……所有的历史经验都证实一点，除非一个人试图抵达“不可能的世界”，他将无法实现“可能的世界”。秦晖先生所坚守的，或许正是这种在“不可能”面前不断开拓“可能”的勇气。

USNI 新闻图 这些是根据海军和公开数据，截至 2026 年 11 月 2 日，美国海军在世界各地部署的航母打击群和两栖战备群的大致位置。如果 CSG 或 ARG 正在进行分类操作，图表会反映主力舰的位置。正在部署的总战力 286（USS 228、USNS 58） 104（USS 73、USNS 31）（46 FDNF、58 轮换） 76（58 部署、18 本地）在日本 分配到第 13 海军陆战队远征部队的美国海军陆战队在黄蜂级两栖攻击舰 USS 上观察日本硫磺岛马金岛 (LHD-8)，日期为 2026 年 10 月 24 日，发布日期为 2026 年 11 月 1 日。美国海军陆战队照片 USS Tripoli (LHA-7) 正在日本佐世保港口。两栖攻击舰马金岛号（LHD-8）位于日本横须贺。马金岛两栖准备大队包括马金岛、安克雷奇号航空母舰 (LPD-23)、约翰·P·穆萨号航空母舰 (LPD-26) 和已上船的第 13 海军陆战队远征部队。 2026 年 10 月 30 日，亨利·J·凯撒级舰队补给加油船蒂佩卡努号 (T-AO-199) 与尼米兹级航空母舰西奥多·罗斯福号 (CVN-71) 进行海上补给。美国海军照片 西奥多·罗斯福号航空母舰 (CVN-71) 参加“利剑”演习后正在南海进行补给27. 多边演习于周四结束。

title: Marine Force-Southeast Asia Will Maintain Continuous Presence in the Philippines
zh_title: 东南亚海军陆战队将继续在菲律宾保持存在

content:
美国海军陆战队下士2026 年 8 月 25 日，在菲律宾博赫多尔举行的群岛海岸防御连续体 26.4 期间，第一海军陆战队远征军东南亚海军陆战队轮换部队北部海空炮火联络连分遣队的一名火力支援海军陆战队员与菲律宾海军陆战队第四海军旅一起进行火力支援小组训练。该服务上周宣布，东南亚轮换力量目前正在第二次连续轮换到菲律宾。 MRF-SEA 于 10 月 26 日进行了轮换。MRF-SEA 最初是一支为期六个月的轮换部队，从 10 月到 3 月部署到该地区，但其任务在 4 月延长。应菲律宾政府邀请，该部队目前在菲律宾持续驻扎，以继续与菲律宾军方合作。 MRF-SEA 是在第一海军陆战队远征军支持下作战的两支轮换部队之一，另一支是海军陆战队轮换部队-达尔文。与作为海军陆战队空地特遣部队部署的 MRF-D 不同，MRF-SEA 部署为可扩展的特遣部队，其指挥总部是常设组成部分。其他海军陆战队单位将根据需要进行分配。我们。
2026 年 6 月 24 日，为支持 MRF-SEA 而部署的第三濒海战斗队、海军陆战队第三临海团、海军陆战队第三师的海军陆战队士兵和海军陆战队第四旅的菲律宾海军陆战队士兵，在菲律宾巴丹群岛伊特巴亚特的海上关键地形安全行动期间，在地形巡逻的同时参加城市地形军事行动，以支持 KAMANDAG 10。美国海军陆战队照片轮换前 extension, the command element of the MRF-SEA would move between Southeast Asian countries based on where scheduled activities would take place.自四月份以来，指挥部门一直驻扎在菲律宾。目前的部署是 MRF-SEA 的第六次迭代。轮换部署于 2022 年开始。根据海军陆战队的一份新闻稿，该部队的存在旨在加强联合战备和美菲联盟，每次轮换都建立在之前部队的关系和经验教训的基础上，MRF-SEA 称之为“有目的的存在”。 “我们的目标从来都不是简单地出现在菲律宾，”即将卸任的 MRF-SEA 轮换指挥官罗伯特·邦恩 (Robert Bunn) 上校说。 “存在必须有目的。与我们的菲律宾盟友一起进行的每一次演习、计划会议和重复都是一个机会，让我们变得更加具有互操作性、响应能力和能力，并在每次活动中逐渐变得更好。
下一次轮换现在有机会吸取这些教训和关系，推动联盟向前迈进一步。”之前的 MRF-SEA 轮换中，该部队在“肩并肩 26”演习、“卡曼达格 10”演习以及通过群岛海岸防御连续体 (ACDC) 进行的一系列双边活动期间与菲律宾军队一起进行了训练。该连续体在主要演习之间提供了反复训练，使美国和菲律宾部队能够将一次活动中的经验教训应用到下一次活动中。 ACDC是一系列双边训练活动和主题专家交流，支持菲律宾海军陆战队的现代化努力和菲律宾海军陆战队的群岛海岸防御概念，同时加强美国和菲律宾军队之间的联合战备。

U.S. Marine Corps Cpl. Antwon Brooks, a fire support Marine with Air Naval Gunfire Liaison Company Detachment – North, Marine Rotational Force – Southeast Asia, I Marine Expeditionary Force, conducts fire support team training alongside Philippine marines with 4th Marine Brigade, Philippine Marine Corps, during Archipelagic Coastal Defense Continuum 26.4 in Bojeador, Philippines, Aug. 25, 2026. US Marine Corps photo Marine Rotational Force-Southeast Asia is now on its second continuous rotation to the Philippines, the service announced last week. MRF-SEA held a rotation turnover on Oct. 26. MRF-SEA originally began as a six-month rotational force that deployed to the region from October to March but its mission was extended in April . The force is now providing a continuous presence in the Philippines at the invitation of the country’s government to continue cooperation with its military. MRF-SEA is one of two rotational forces operating under the aegis of I Marine Expeditionary Force, with the other being Marine Rotational Force-Darwin. Unlike MRF-D, which deploys as a Marine Air-Ground Task Force, MRF-SEA deploys as a scalable task force with its command headquarters being the permanent component. Other Marine units are assigned as and when required. U.S. Marines assigned to 3rd Littoral Combat Team, 3rd Marine Littoral Regiment, 3rd Marine Division, which deployed to support MRF-SEA, and Philippine marines assigned to 4th Marine Brigade, patrol through terrain while participating in military operations in urban terrain training during maritime key terrain security operations in support of KAMANDAG 10 at Itbayat, Batanes islands, Philippines, June 24, 2026. US Marine Corps photo Before the rotation extension, the command element of the MRF-SEA would move between Southeast Asian countries based on where scheduled activities would take place. Since April, the command element has been based in the Philippines The current deployment is the sixth iteration of MRF-SEA. The rotational deployment began in 2022. The unit’s presence is designed to strengthen combined readiness and the U.S.-Philippine Alliance, according to a Marine Corps news release, with each rotation building on the relationships and lessons of the force before in an approach MRF-SEA calls “presence with purpose.” “Our goal was never simply to be present in the Philippines,” said Col. Robert Bunn, commanding officer of the outgoing MRF-SEA rotation. “Presence has to have purpose. Every exercise, planning session and repetition alongside our Philippine allies was an opportunity to become more interoperable, responsive and capable together, progressively getting better with each event. The next rotation now has the opportunity to take those lessons and relationships to move the alliance another step forward.” The previous rotation of MRF-SEA saw the force train alongside Philippine troops during Balikatan 26, KAMANDAG 10 and a series of bilateral events through the Archipelagic Coastal Defense Continuum (ACDC). The continuum provided recurring training between major exercises, allowing U.S. and Philippine forces to apply lessons from one event to the next. ACDC is is a series of bilateral training activities and subject matter expert exchanges that support Philippine Marine Corps modernization efforts and the Philippine Marine Corps’ Archipelagic Coastal Defense Concept along with strengthening combined readiness between U.S. and Philippine forces Training throughout the previous MRF-SEA rotation included command and control, sensing, fires integration, maritime domain awareness, aviation, communications and unmanned systems. Marines also tested how forces and equipment could move, communicate and operate across the Philippines’ distributed and archipelagic terrain. This included testing the mobility of the AN/TPS-80 Ground/Air Task-Oriented Radar as part of ACDC training and movement of the Navy-Marine Expeditionary Ship Interdiction System (NMESIS) and Marine Air Defense Integrated System (MADIS) from ports to distributed exercise locations as part of KAMANDAG 10. U.S. Marines assigned to 3rd Littoral Anti-Air Battalion, 3rd Marine Littoral Regiment, 3rd Marine Division, drive a Marine Air Defense Integrated System off a Philippine surface connector in support of maritime key terrain security operations during KAMANDAG 10 at Calayan, Philippines, June 22, 2026. US Marine Corps photo The incoming rotation will continue the progression of the U.S.-Philippine partnership through ACDC and Exercise Balikatan 27, according to the release. Training will continue to focus on operating across distributed and archipelagic terrain, strengthening the ability of U.S. and Philippine forces to coordinate, maneuver and sustain operations across geographically dispersed locations. Marines and sailors will also continue bilateral humanitarian assistance, disaster response and crisis response training. “Our Marines and sailors are inheriting more than a mission, they are inheriting momentum,” said Col. Coby Moran, commanding officer of the incoming MRF-SEA rotation. “We will build on the relationships, lessons and interoperability developed by the Marines and sailors before us and continue working shoulder-to-shoulder with our Philippine allies.” Moran previously operated in the Philippines, leading a I MEF technical assistance and advisory team in April that oversaw a maritime prepositioning force offload at the Port of Cagayan de Oro, Mindanao, Philippines. The event was the first MPF offload at Mindanao, according to a Marine Corps news release at the time . The offload saw roll-on/roll-off cargo ship USNS Sgt. William W. Seay (T-AKR-302) transport vehicles and equipment to I MEF, which was preparing for Exercise Balikatan 26 in the Philippines. “MPF operations are a unique capability of the Marine Corps,” said Moran in the release. “They allow us to deliver capabilities anywhere in the world, providing critical combat power to Marine air-ground task force commanders.” The Marine Corps has not disclosed whether MRF-SEA will now only focus on the Philippines or whether it will continue leading Marine Corps engagement and activities with other countries in the region alongside its activities in the Philippines.

title: How China Might Target US Midterms

summary: 没有研究表明中国的宣传或虚假信息在中期选举中发挥了关键作用，特别是与俄罗斯的侵略性尝试相比。然而，存在重大盲点。如果愿意的话，北京完全有能力通过微信应用程序和中国的人工智能模型来塑造政治辩论。北京的目标可能不是转移对国会的控制权，而是减少已知的共产党批评者的存在，特别是那些在国会及行政部门中国委员会任职的人。该委员会由国会于 2000 年 10 月成立，负责监督中国的经济活动

没有研究表明中国的宣传或虚假信息在中期选举中发挥了关键作用，特别是与俄罗斯的侵略性尝试相比。然而，存在重大盲点。如果愿意的话，北京完全有能力通过微信应用程序和中国的人工智能模型来塑造政治辩论。北京的目标可能不是转移对国会的控制权，而是减少已知的共产党批评者的存在，特别是那些在国会及行政部门中国委员会任职的人。该委员会由国会于 2000 年 10 月成立，负责监督中国的人权和法治。委员会成员参加了几场竞争激烈的竞选，其中包括俄亥俄州前参议员谢罗德·布朗和阿拉斯加现任委员会主席丹·沙利文。爱荷华州和弗吉尼亚州的众议院竞选涉及现任委员会成员扎克·纳恩和珍·基甘斯。正在竞选爱荷华州参议员的阿什利·辛森 (Ashley Hinson) 是众议院中国共产党特别委员会的成员，这是另一个批评该政权的国会机构。由于不同的原因，德克萨斯州看起来特别敏感。微信是一款消息传递和多功能应用程序，估计有 150 万美国用户，主要集中在华裔人口众多的州。华裔美国人约占德克萨斯州人口的百分之一。中国政府对微信的审查是有据可查的。
德克萨斯大学 2025 年的一项研究基于对德克萨斯州 20 名华裔美国人的采访，详细介绍了政治错误信息如何在该平台上传播。 一位年轻的受访者描述了她的父亲如何在实际选举前几个月读到一名亚裔美国女性当选波士顿市长。 “他只是接受他读到的所有内容，然后转发，”她说。 “我婆婆也是。”文化和社会压力降低了纠正家人或朋友群体中的错误信息的意愿。 “我感觉不对长辈说坏话，尤其是在群聊环境中，”一名 19 岁的华裔美国人解释道。在这种环境下，该应用程序的功能就很强大。 “很多人不知道该投票给谁，所以很容易受到影响，”另一位受访者评论道。 “这是一个很大的政治平台，很多人都会盲目跟随。”获取最新注册以定期接收带宽电子邮件并随时了解 CEPA 的工作情况。

No research shows Chinese propaganda or disinformation playing a pivotal role in the midterm elections, particularly when compared to Russia’s aggressive attempts. Yet significant blind spots exist. If it desired, Beijing is well-positioned to shape political debate through the WeChat app and through Chinese AI models. Rather than shifting control of Congress, Beijing’s goal would likely be to reduce the presence of known Communist Party critics, particularly those serving in the Congressional-Executive Commission on China. Created by Congress in October 2000, the Commission monitors Chinese human rights and rule of law. Several competitive races feature Commission members, including former Senator Sherrod Brown in Ohio and current Commission Chair Dan Sullivan in Alaska. House races in Iowa and Virginia involve current Commission members Zach Nunn and Jen Kiggans. Ashley Hinson, who is running for the Senate in Iowa, is on the House Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party, another Congressional body critical of the regime. Texas looks particularly sensitive for a different reason. WeChat , a messaging and multi-function app, has an estimated 1.5 million US users, concentrated in states with large Chinese American populations. Chinese Americans  make up roughly one percent of  Texas’s population .  Chinese state-sponsored censorship  on WeChat is well-documented. A 2025 University of Texas study based on interviews with 20 Chinese Americans in Texas detailed how political misinformation circulates on the platform. One young interviewee described how her father read that an Asian American woman had been elected mayor of Boston months before the actual election. “He just accepts everything he reads, and then he just forwards it,” she said. “My mother-in-law, too.” Cultural and social pressures reduce willingness to correct misinformation in family or friend groups. “It doesn’t feel right for me to talk bad to my elders, especially in the group chat setting,” a 19-year-old Chinese American explained. In this environment, the app is powerful. “A lot of people don’t know who to vote for, so they are easily swayed,” another interviewee commented. “It is a big political platform, and a lot of people will just blindly follow.” Get the Latest Sign up to receive regular Bandwidth emails and stay informed about CEPA's work. The 2026 elections are the first to take place in an environment where AI chatbots are widely available. About one-fifth of Americans plan to use AI tools to help learn about candidates or inform voting decisions, according to a recent survey . Most will turn to American models such as ChatGPT, Claude, Grok, or Perplexity, but many US developers are increasingly relying on Chinese-origin models such as DeepSeek and Qwen, allowing them to enter the US information environment. These models reflect the Chinese government’s official stances on domestic politics and human rights. Censorship and propaganda have also been found  in responses to questions about US press freedom and elections. One study examined Chinese AI models’ responses to questions about the upcoming US elections. Conducted by a research group based in Europe, researchers tested seven AI models (five US and two Chinese) with a set of 20 polling-style questions. All models proved relatively consistent and offered mixed results in terms of partisan preferences. The two Chinese models did not diverge sharply from their US counterparts in their responses. DeepSeek, for example, selected the Democratic option on two questions about which party’s candidate it would select for Congress and which party it prefers to control Congress. So did Claude and Perplexity (99% on one of the questions). By contrast, Qwen chose Democrats 55% and 75% of the time, respectively. The results are striking for what they show about the leeway allowed the Chinese models to comment on US versus Chinese politics. DeepSeek offered critical assessments of the US president’s job performance. Asking the same questions about Chinese President Xi Jinping would almost certainly produce refusals or strictly glowing reviews. Major holes remain in our understanding of where and how Chinese Communist Party-linked electoral influence could be occurring. Researchers, election monitors, and others focused on election integrity should address these gaps — particularly before the 2028 elections. 这标志着中亚的军事采购总体上摆脱了对俄罗斯的严重依赖，俄罗斯喜欢将该地区视为自己的后院。印度并不是中亚国家唯一求助的参与者。例如，中国在过去几年中通过向乌兹别克斯坦出售成都歼10CE喷气式飞机来扩大其在该地区的地位，乌兹别克斯坦是继巴基斯坦之后第二个接收飞机的国家。据报道，哈萨克斯坦也有兴趣从中国购买六架K-8W轻型战斗机。还有土耳其，其紧凑型无人机在纳戈尔诺-卡拉巴赫战争以及乌克兰和伊朗持续冲突中的表现对中亚国家越来越有吸引力。尽管印度对中亚的武器销售仍然相对较少，但中国武器在该地区的存在不断增加，表明该地区的力量平衡可能发生重大的长期变化。自20世纪90年代以来，俄罗斯一直是中亚国家的主要军事和安全伙伴，这一地位体现在其广泛的军事基地网络、双边防务协议和多边安全安排上。获取最新注册以接收定期电子邮件并随时了解 CEPA 的工作。

While attention mostly falls upon China’s inroads into Central Asia’s economic and security spheres, so undercutting Russia, India has emerged as a new seller of weapons as the region diversifies its military procurement. In early October, Indian Defense Secretary Rajesh Kumar Singh confirmed that India had exported its domestically developed Akash air-defense system to Tajikistan. The system can intercept aircraft, helicopters, and drones at ranges of up to approximately 25 km (16 miles). New Delhi also confirmed the export of the same system to Turkmenistan, which had previously been reliant on Russian- and Chinese-origin air-defense equipment. Cooperation has also expanded in other security fields. In September-October, India and Kazakhstan held the Kazind-2026 joint military exercise involving approximately 60 military personnel from each country. This followed the India-Uzbekistan exercises, Dustlik-2026, held in April and a similar drill held with Kyrgyzstan. India has likewise stepped up security coordination and counterterrorism efforts, military-technical consultations, and intelligence-related cooperation with Uzbekistan, Kyrgyzstan, and Tajikistan. The India-Central Asia foreign ministers’ security dialogue held in June 2025 in New Delhi reaffirmed cooperation against terrorism, terrorist financing, arms trafficking, and narcotics trafficking. India’s inroads matter. It signals a general shift in Central Asia’s military procurement away from a heavy dependence on Russia, which likes to regard the region as its backyard. India is not the only actor Central Asian countries are turning to. China, for example, has in the past few years expanded its position in the region by selling Chengdu J-10CE jets to Uzbekistan, the second country to take delivery after Pakistan. Kazakhstan is also reportedly interested in purchasing six K-8W light-combat aircraft from China. There is also Turkey with its compact drones that have become increasingly attractive for Central Asian countries following their performance in the wars for Nagorno-Karabakh, and amid the ongoing conflicts in Ukraine and Iran. Although Indian arms sales to Central Asia remain relatively modest, the growing presence of Chinese weaponry in the region points to a potentially significant long-term shift in the regional balance of power. Since the 1990s, Russia has served as the predominant military and security partner for Central Asian states, a position reflected in its extensive network of military bases, bilateral defense agreements, and multilateral security arrangements. Russian domination of Central Asia’s military procurement began to change in the early 2020s, particularly following Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. The prolonged conflict has placed considerable strain on Russia’s military-industrial capacity, limiting Moscow’s ability to meet the defense requirements of its traditional partners. Russia has consequently faced growing difficulties in fulfilling arms orders and supplying military equipment to allies and partners, including Belarus, Armenia, and several Central Asian states. These constraints have prompted Central Asian governments to diversify military procurement, creating new opportunities for India to expand its defense exports and strengthen security cooperation across the five republics. Although Russia remains an important military partner, India’s growing role and that of China could gradually erode Moscow’s position. More importantly, the implications of this trend extend beyond the immediate sale of military equipment. The acquisition of Indian weapons systems creates longer-term technological and logistical ties, as recipient countries will require Indian expertise, spare parts, maintenance services, technical training, and modernization support. Over time, these dependencies could translate into deeper institutional ties between Indian defense industries and Central Asian armed forces. Seen from a wider perspective, India’s military outreach to Central Asia is part of New Delhi’s search for more active relations with the region. The engagement increasingly consists of developing regional trade routes (especially on the north-south axis), bilateral commerce, investments into critical infrastructure and cooperation on potential security spillover from Afghanistan, all of them exemplified in the visits made by Indian prime minister Narendra Modi to Uzbekistan and Kyrgyzstan earlier this year. New Delhi and Tashkent elevated their relationship to a comprehensive strategic partnership and agreed to work on connectivity, education and, most of all, critical minerals. Indian weaponry, coupled with that of other non-traditional suppliers, creates a qualitatively different balance of power in Central Asia. What currently appears to be a relatively limited expansion of Indian arms exports could eventually become an important driver of a broader redistribution of military and security influence in Central Asia, gradually challenging Moscow’s and, to a certain extent, Beijing’s influence in the region.
