Hong Kong police 'Sharp Eye' scheme to expand to private malls this year
Hong Kong police say their 'Sharp Eye' CCTV network will expand to private premises this year, with several malls agreeing to connect their cameras. Senior police officer Leung Ming-lap says the scheme meets legal and security standards.
6 Nov 2026 at 00:23 HKT · updated 6 Nov, 04:25 · 1 min read
Hong Kong police have announced that their 'Sharp Eye' surveillance scheme will expand to private premises this year, with several shopping malls already agreeing to connect their closed-circuit television (CCTV) systems to the network.
Senior Superintendent Leung Ming-lap of the force's operations division said the response from malls during discussions had been positive, with many expressing interest in joining the scheme. He attributed this to the scheme's proven effectiveness in solving cases and preventing crime, as well as the added layer of security it provides for malls that already have their own CCTV systems.
Leung said police had consulted legal experts and third-party bodies to ensure the scheme meets all regulatory and oversight requirements. Asked whether malls would need to add signage informing the public of the connection, he said police encouraged such measures to help people understand the crime-prevention benefits and increase their sense of safety.
The senior superintendent noted that connecting mall CCTV systems to 'Sharp Eye' would save time and manpower in future investigations, as police would no longer need to apply separately to each location for footage or find someone familiar with each system.
When asked about the risk of hackers accessing data collected by 'Sharp Eye' through a mall's CCTV system, Leung said the scheme's information security meets the government's highest standards. He added that authorities had invested heavily in a dedicated fibre-optic network for the scheme, making the risk of data theft very low.
According to sources, the malls involved include Olympia City and Tuen Mun Town Plaza, both owned by the Sino Group; Kwai Chung Commercial Plaza, under the Housing Authority; and The Latitude in Fanling, managed by the Housing Society.

content:
香港警方本月将在闭路电视系统中添加人工智能面部识别中国劳工公告栏
星期五, 6 十一月 2026 · 香港 香港和中国劳工新闻英文版
香港警方本月将在闭路电视系统中添加人工智能面部识别功能
香港警方本月将在其“Sharp Eye”闭路电视系统中添加人工智能面部识别功能。官员们表示，这项技术已经帮助找到了一名失踪的老人并逮捕了一名抢劫嫌疑人，预计到 2028 年将配备 60,000 个摄像头。
2026 年 11 月 6 日，香港时间 00:11 · 更新于 11 月 6 日，04:25 · 阅读时间 1 分钟
香港警方将于本月在其“锐眼”闭路电视系统中添加人工智能面部识别功能，预计到 2028 年，全市所有 60,000 个摄像头都将配备该功能。高级官员表示，由于计算能力的限制，该技术不会在每个摄像头上同时使用。
警方表示，面部识别功能的测试已经证明是成功的。在一个案例中，警方在接到报告后约 90 分钟内找到了一名患有痴呆症的 80 岁男子。在另一个例子中，系统识别了一名抢劫嫌疑人的面部特征，并检测到他在犯罪后的动作，从而将其逮捕。
警队行动部高级警司梁铭良表示，采用面部识别技术相当于增派警员昼夜不停地监视闭路电视，以发现失踪人员和可疑人员。他表示，这项技术将加快调查速度，减少警员手动查看大量录像的需要，从而可以将更多人员部署到其他职责中。
梁振英表示，面部识别技术准确，是一种成熟、可靠的调查工具，已被中国大陆和海外的执法机构使用。为了保护个人资料和隐私，系统在使用前需要授权，由经过专门培训的人员提出申请，并经督察级以上人员批准。使用后，将进行审查。
截至上月底，“锐眼”项目已帮助破获刑事案件2192起。 Leung表示，由于成本和法律要求，图像的存储时间不会超过31天，而面部识别数据的保留时间不会超过180天。

Friday, 6 Nov 2026 · Hong Kong Hong Kong and China labour news in English
Hong Kong police to add AI facial recognition to CCTV system this month
Hong Kong police will add AI facial recognition to its 'Sharp Eye' CCTV system this month. Officials say the technology has already helped locate a missing elderly man and arrest a robbery suspect, with 60,000 cameras expected to be equipped by 2028.
6 Nov 2026 at 00:11 HKT · updated 6 Nov, 04:25 · 1 min read
Hong Kong police will add artificial intelligence facial recognition to their 'Sharp Eye' CCTV system this month, with all 60,000 cameras across the city expected to be equipped with the function by 2028. Senior officers said the technology would not be used simultaneously on every camera due to computing power constraints.
Police said tests of the facial recognition function have already proven successful. In one case, officers located an 80-year-old man with dementia within about 90 minutes of receiving a report. In another instance, the system identified a robbery suspect's facial features and detected his movements after the crime, leading to an arrest.
Senior Superintendent Leung Ming-leung of the Force Operations Department described the introduction of facial recognition as equivalent to having additional officers working around the clock to monitor CCTV feeds for missing persons and suspicious individuals. He said the technology would speed up investigations and reduce the need for officers to manually review large amounts of footage, allowing more personnel to be deployed to other duties.
Leung said the facial recognition technology is accurate and a mature, reliable investigative tool already used by law enforcement agencies in mainland China and overseas. To protect personal data and privacy, the system requires authorisation before use, with applications made by specially trained personnel and approved by officers of inspector rank or above. After use, a review will be conducted.
As of the end of last month, the Sharp Eye programme had helped solve 2,192 criminal cases. Leung said that due to cost and legal requirements, images will not be stored for more than 31 days, while facial recognition data will be retained for no longer than 180 days.

巴基斯坦将一个中国政策带入其领空
有报道称，巴基斯坦上个月禁止两家台湾航空公司——其国有航空公司中华航空公司和私营航空公司长荣航空公司——在其领空过境，这引发了人们对伊斯兰堡对“一个中国”政策的解释以及北京对其决策的影响程度的质疑。巴基斯坦国防部长卡瓦贾·阿西夫表示（在新窗口中打开）：“航空部门遵循一个中国政策，只允许中国大陆进入。”鉴于即使中国大陆也不对台湾商业航空公司实施此类限制，这一举措就显得更加不寻常。
该禁令突然被撤销，两家航空公司均获准在 2027 年 3 月 27 日之前进入巴基斯坦领空。然而，这只是临时安排，对于截止日期后会发生什么没有给出任何解释。
鉴于即使中国大陆也不对台湾商业航空公司实施此类限制，这一举措就显得更加不寻常。
巴基斯坦和台湾几乎没有实质性联系。伊斯兰堡严格奉行一个中国政策，与中国保持“铁杆友谊”。巴基斯坦与台湾的联系有限，居住在那里的巴基斯坦国民 (在新窗口中打开) 仅有 900 多名，其中包括学生、餐馆老板和其他专业人士。没有代表处，也从来没有设立过。两国之间也没有直航航班。南亚与台湾之间唯一的空中航线是台北至德里航线 (Opens in new window)，计划于 12 月 1 日恢复。
这项禁令超出了巴基斯坦遵守一个中国政策的通常要求。伊斯兰堡是其最坚定的追随者之一，定期重申（在新窗口中打开）其承诺并无条件支持中国的主权和领土完整，包括其在台湾问题上的立场。冒着使复杂问题简单化的风险，像巴基斯坦那样严格遵守，通常意味着反对台湾独立，接受北京关于台湾是中国一部分的主张，并且不与台北保持官方关系。然而，各国对政策的解释不同（在新窗口中打开）。一些坚持它的人仍然在台湾保持着贸易联系和非官方办事处。该政策并不意味着各国拒绝允许台湾商业航空公司过境其领空。这种许可是民航安排的问题。
各国以政治理由限制台湾航班。今年4月，塞舌尔、毛里求斯和马达加斯加撤回了台湾现任总统赖清德计划前往台湾在非洲仅存的外交盟友斯威士兰的飞越许可。但是，限制总统飞行是一个整体

|Pakistan takes the One China policy into its airspace
Pakistan takes the One China policy into its airspace
Reports that Pakistan had last month barred two Taiwanese airlines, its state carrier China Airlines and private carrier EVA Air, from transiting through its airspace raised questions about Islamabad’s interpretation of the One China policy and the extent of Beijing’s influence over its decisions. Pakistan’s Defence Minister Khawaja Asif said (Opens in new window), “The aviation division follows the One China policy, only mainland China is allowed.” The move was all the more unusual given that even China does not impose such restrictions on Taiwanese commercial airlines.
The ban was abruptly reversed, with both airlines granted access to Pakistani airspace until 27 March 2027. This is only a temporary arrangement, however, and no explanation has been given about what happens after the deadline.
The move was all the more unusual given that even China does not impose such restrictions on Taiwanese commercial airlines.
Pakistan and Taiwan have few substantive ties. Islamabad strictly adheres to the One China policy and maintains an “ironclad friendship” with China. Pakistan’s limited links with Taiwan include just over 900 Pakistani nationals (Opens in new window) living there, including students, restaurant owners and other professionals. There is no representative office, nor has there ever been one. There are also no direct flights between the two sides. The only air connection between South Asia and Taiwan is the Taipei–Delhi route (Opens in new window), which is scheduled to resume on 1 December.
The ban goes beyond what Pakistan’s adherence to the One China policy would normally require. Islamabad is among its strongest adherents, regularly reaffirming (Opens in new window) its commitment and unconditionally supporting China’s sovereignty and territorial integrity, including its position on Taiwan. At the risk of simplifying a complex issue, a strict adherence, like that of Pakistan’s, generally means opposing Taiwan’s independence, accepting Beijing’s claim that Taiwan is part of China, and not maintaining official ties with Taipei. However, countries interpret (Opens in new window) the policy differently. Some that adhere to it still maintain trade ties and unofficial offices in Taiwan. The policy does not entail that countries deny Taiwanese commercial airlines permission to transit through their airspace. Such permission is a matter of civil aviation arrangements.
Countries have restricted Taiwanese flights on political grounds. In April this year, Seychelles, Mauritius and Madagascar withdrew overflight permissions (Opens in new window) for Taiwan’s incumbent President Lai Ching-te’s planned trip to Eswatini, Taiwan’s only remaining diplomatic ally in Africa. But, restricting a presidential flight is an entirely different issue from denying overflight rights to commercial airlines.
China Airlines flight from Taipei, 19 October 2026 (cifraser1/Flickr)
So, what could have prompted the decision? Was it an extension of China’s grey-zone activities (Opens in new window), or a show of loyalty arising from the China-Pakistan all-weather friendship?
There are two possible explanations for Pakistan’s decision. The first is that China asked Pakistan to impose the ban to reinforce the One China policy, discourage international engagement with Taiwan and demonstrate Beijing’s influence over its partners. Pakistan remains one of China’s most reliable supporters of its position on Taiwan.
The second possibility is that Pakistan imposed the ban on its own initiative to show its loyalty to China, particularly at a time when it is seeking closer ties with the United States. The Mecca Pact may have added to Islamabad’s incentive to reassure Beijing. Meanwhile, the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor, a flagship component of the Belt and Road Initiative, has become a security liability (Opens in new window) rather than a strategic and economic asset for Beijing. Against this backdrop, the ban may have been a token gesture to show that Pakistan’s efforts to move closer to Washington have not come at the expense of its relationship with China. Although overflight permissions have since been restored, at least for the time being, the message to Beijing is already delivered.
Pakistani airspace is useful for Taiwanese flights travelling to Middle East and Europe. If there is a renewed ban after the March 2027 deadline, it may not have major long-term implications for Taiwan, but rerouting would add to the duration and cost of operating these routes. The episode is also a reminder that Pakistan wants to remain useful to China and is willing to demonstrate that usefulness through decisions affecting Taiwan.
The greater concern is whether this sets a precedent. China could use similar pressure to influence other countries that are close to Beijing and strongly adhere to the One China policy, creating problems for Taiwanese airlines, particularly given Taipei’s lack of representation in the International Civil Aviation Organisation (ICAO). Restrictions on commercial aviation can potentially become another means of exerting pressure on Taiwan.
The decision is further evidence of China’s already formidable influence over Pakistan and Islamabad’s willingness to go further in demonstrating its loyalty to Beijing. But it does little for Pakistan. Applying the One China policy to commercial aviation imposes a restriction with little benefit beyond political signalling. More problematic is Pakistan’s readiness to extend its interpretation of the policy into areas not traditionally associated with it, adding new dimensions to and further complicating an already complex issue.
Sana Hashmi, PhD, is a fellow at the Taiwan-Asia Exchange Foundation. Views are personal.
